sections.heading: Comparing calculator policy across the qualifications
paragraphs: This is a small comparison with a large consequence and it is almost never made. In both IGCSE mathematics specifications, calculators are permitted throughout. In IB Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level, one paper is sat without one. That single difference accounts for a recognisable pattern of failure in the first term of the Diploma.

A student who has had a calculator available for every mathematics examination since the age of eleven develops a particular set of habits. Exact values in trigonometry are looked up rather than known. Surd manipulation is avoided because a decimal is always available. Index laws are applied through the machine rather than by hand. Mental arithmetic becomes slow. None of those cost a single mark at IGCSE, and all of them cost marks in the Diploma.

The implication for a Year 11 student in Deira who is heading for IB Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches is a specific and cheap piece of preparation: short, frequent non-calculator drills through the spring term, on exact trigonometric values, surds, indices and algebraic manipulation. Six to eight weeks of a few minutes a day builds the habit that the Diploma will assume. It does nothing for the IGCSE grade, which is why nobody suggests it, and it is one of the highest-value things a family can do at that point.

For a student heading to A Level the comparison is less stark, since calculator policy there varies by paper, but the underlying fluency argument holds. The general rule across all four qualifications on this page: the better a student's algebra by hand, the easier everything after IGCSE becomes, and IGCSE itself will never force them to build it.

sections.heading: Why the delivery answer is the same on every side of these comparisons
paragraphs: Having run four comparisons, it is worth noting what none of them changed. Whether a student is on 0580 or 4MA1, Core or Extended, taking Additional Mathematics or not, heading for A Levels or the Diploma, the requirement is identical: a tutor who has taught that exact specification and tier, available at an hour the student can actually use, with a working surface that keeps the question, the working and the correction visible together.

The first of those is a supply problem. Specialist supply in Dubai is thin and distributed by where tutors live rather than by where demand is, and a radius around Deira is a poor filter for a qualification code. Matching from the whole available pool is what makes it possible to say yes to a 4MA1 Higher request in one week and a 0606 Additional Mathematics request in the next.

The second is a scheduling problem specific to this district. Students travel out of Deira to school, arrival home is late and variable, and in dense apartment housing the quiet hour moves from day to day. A session set from dismissal time fails; a session set from arrival and from when a room is actually free holds. Online delivery is what makes that adjustable, including moving the sustained work to a weekend morning when the flat is quieter.

The third is pedagogical and specific to mathematics. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. On a shared whiteboard both people write, the student's own working is preserved rather than erased, and the board is saved so the next session opens where the last one stopped. For a subject that is almost entirely about watching a pen move and catching the step where it goes wrong, that is better than a single sheet of paper. Where a tutor in the room is genuinely needed, the Dubai market supplies it at the rates above.

process.title: Send the code and the tier
process.description: 0580 Extended, 4MA1 Higher, 0606, 4PM1 — whichever appears on the entry form, plus the tier. That single sheet determines which past papers are useful and is the cheapest quality control available to a parent in this subject.

process.title: Ask the school about the tier deadline
process.description: In writing: which tier, on what evidence, and what is the deadline for changing it. Before that date a tutoring plan can aim at a tier move, which is the largest lever available. After it, the plan aims at performance within the papers already chosen.

process.title: Free trial lesson before payment
process.description: One free trial lesson before any payment, with the most recent marked paper open. Ask the tutor which specification they have taught by code, and ask them to mark a page aloud saying what each annotation is worth.

process.title: One or two targets, written down
process.description: The plan names at most two topic areas or one habit, the school assessment it is aimed at, and the evidence that will show it worked. If the fourth mathematics paper is in play, the plan says which of the two qualifications gets the session and why.

process.title: Reviewed on a timed paper
process.description: The review point is a complete past paper on the correct specification, sat to time and marked together. That is also the only honest way to measure problem solving across topics, which is what separates grades at the top of either tier.

whyPoints.title: Matched by code, not by subject name
whyPoints.description: 0580 Extended and 4MA1 Higher are different papers with different question-length distributions, and 0606 is a different qualification altogether. We ask for the code first, because past-paper work on the wrong board trains pacing a student cannot use.

whyPoints.title: The tier treated as the main variable
whyPoints.description: The tier sets the grade ceiling and the content, and it is decided on earlier attainment with a deadline attached. We will tell you when a move is worth evidencing and, equally, when moving a student up would convert a comfortable grade into a poor one.

whyPoints.title: Priorities set by marks, not by chapters
whyPoints.description: Revision usually follows textbook order. Ours follows the marks: algebraic manipulation first because four other topics depend on it, then the reliably-missed narrow topics, then full papers for problem solving across topics.

whyPoints.title: Honest about the fourth paper
whyPoints.description: Additional Mathematics and Further Pure are genuinely good preparation for post-16 mathematics and genuinely heavy in a Year 11 week. We will say when a strong single grade is the better outcome, which is not the advice that sells more sessions.

whyPoints.title: The band matched to the job
whyPoints.description: Budget-band supervision for consistency, qualified band for content, specialist band for diagnosis and tier judgement. Buying the wrong band is the commonest waste in this subject, and the table on this page says which is which with sources.

whyPoints.title: A whiteboard built for working
whyPoints.description: Mathematics needs the question, the working and the correction visible at once and preserved between sessions. A shared digital whiteboard does that; a single sheet of paper does not. This is the subject where online delivery is an advantage rather than a convenience.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether my child sits 0580 or 4MA1?
faqs.answer: For progression, no; both are accepted on the same basis. For revision, substantially. Cambridge 0580 spreads marks across more, shorter items while Pearson 4MA1 uses fewer, longer questions, so pacing practice differs and a student who has drilled the wrong board's papers will find the real paper unfamiliar for reasons unrelated to the mathematics. Tiering language differs too: Core and Extended against Foundation and Higher. Get the exact code from the entry form and give it to any tutor before the first session.

faqs.question: Which is harder, Cambridge Extended or Pearson Higher?
faqs.answer: Neither in any general sense, and the question usually masks a better one: which suits this student. A student who works quickly and accurately across many short items tends to do better on the Cambridge pattern. A student who reasons well across a long multi-part problem but is slow to start tends to do better on the Pearson pattern. Since the school chooses the board, the practical use of this comparison is to know which weakness to train rather than which qualification to prefer.

faqs.question: How do I find out my child's maths tier and whether it can change?
faqs.answer: Ask the school in writing, naming mathematics specifically, and ask three things: which tier, on what evidence, and what is the deadline for changing it. Tiers are allocated on Year 9 and Year 10 attainment and the realistic window to move is early in Year 10. The tier caps the grade available and determines the content, so a tutoring plan written without it may be targeting topics your child will never be examined on. Get the answer before paying anybody.

faqs.question: Should we push for a move up to Extended or Higher?
faqs.answer: Only on readiness, not on ambition. Upper-tier papers cover additional content and give fewer easy marks, with unstructured multi-step questions that assume a student can combine topics unprompted. A student moved up before they can do that converts a comfortable middle grade into a poor one. The honest test is whether they can attempt a multi-topic problem without being told which topics are involved. If they can, the move is worth evidencing to the school before the entry deadline.

faqs.question: What is Cambridge Additional Mathematics and should my child take it?
faqs.answer: It is a separate qualification, code 0606, taken alongside IGCSE Mathematics by stronger students, covering calculus, trigonometric identities, functions and series at a level closer to the start of A Level. Pearson's equivalent is Further Pure Mathematics, 4PM1. Both make post-16 mathematics materially easier. The cost is workload in a Year 11 week already carrying eight or nine subjects. A strong grade in the main qualification with no fourth paper beats two mediocre results.

faqs.question: Which single topic should we fix first in IGCSE maths?
faqs.answer: Algebraic manipulation, in almost every case, because it is the machinery every other topic uses. A student weak at rearranging and factorising loses marks in equations, functions, trigonometry and mensuration, and will experience that as four separate problems rather than one. After that, the reliably-missed narrow topics are worth a session each: area and volume scale factors, histograms with unequal class widths, reverse percentages, and vector reasoning without a diagram.

faqs.question: Why does my child lose marks on similar shapes questions?
faqs.answer: Because they apply the length scale factor where the question wants the area or volume scale factor. If lengths scale by a factor, areas scale by its square and volumes by its cube, and students who have learned the rule as words rather than as a habit revert to the length factor under pressure. It is the single most reliably missed topic in the syllabus in both specifications, it costs marks every series, and it is genuinely fixable in one or two sessions.

faqs.question: How do histograms with unequal intervals catch students out?
faqs.answer: They read frequency off the vertical axis, when the axis shows frequency density and frequency is the area of the bar. Because most earlier work involves equal class widths where the distinction never arises, students arrive at the topic with a habit that is wrong only in this one case. One session covering frequency density in both directions — reading from a histogram and drawing one — is usually enough, which makes it one of the cheapest mark recoveries available.

faqs.question: Is self-study with past papers enough for IGCSE maths?
faqs.answer: For content revision and timing, often yes, provided two things: the papers are from the correct specification and tier, and the student marks against the official mark scheme rather than checking final answers. Most Dubai schools publish both on their learning platform. Where self-study reliably fails is in diagnosing a habit, because a student who omits method marks cannot see what is missing. That specific job is what a one-to-one hour is for, and it does not need to be weekly.

faqs.question: Is a group class in Al Qusais worth considering for maths?
faqs.answer: Yes, particularly where the problem is consistency rather than understanding. A small group at well below one-to-one rates, taught by somebody who knows the specification, supplies structure and pace, and the Al Qusais and Al Nahda belt has the highest concentration of centres near Deira. What it cannot do is work on one student's specific error pattern, since the class moves at the group's speed. The sensible pattern is a group class for structure and occasional one-to-one for diagnosis.

faqs.question: How much should we pay for IGCSE maths help in Deira?
faqs.answer: Match the band to the job rather than to the subject. Published October 2026 figures: budget online generalists AED 33 to 65 an hour, which is appropriate for supervised Year 9 and Year 10 practice; qualified subject tutors AED 150 to 300, which is right for teaching a genuine topic gap; specialists AED 200 to 450 and above for diagnosis and tier judgement. In-home visits run AED 180 to 500 including travel. The premium band above AED 500 is almost never necessary at IGCSE.

faqs.question: Will my child be allowed a calculator in the IGCSE maths exams?
faqs.answer: Yes, in both specifications and in both tiers, calculators are permitted throughout. That is worth knowing not for the IGCSE but for what follows: IB Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level sits one paper without a calculator, and students who have had one available since the age of eleven arrive without exact trigonometric values, surd fluency or confident index work. Short daily non-calculator drills in the spring term of Year 11 are cheap preparation nobody suggests.

faqs.question: Does IGCSE maths prepare a student for IB Maths AA?
faqs.answer: Partly. The algebraic content carries over directly and is the shared prerequisite for both A Level Mathematics and Analysis and Approaches. What IGCSE does not build is non-calculator fluency, experience of extended independent mathematical work of the kind the Diploma exploration requires, or exposure to calculus unless the student takes Additional Mathematics or Further Pure. A student with a known destination can close two of those three in Year 11 at very little cost.

faqs.question: Our flat is busy. Can maths sessions work at the weekend instead?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for sustained work they are better. A full past paper sat to time takes around ninety minutes plus marking, which is unrealistic on a school evening after a long commute into Deira and straightforward on a Friday or Saturday morning when the flat is quieter and the student is fresher. Many families here run one short weekday session for topic work and a fortnightly weekend session for timed papers, which is also the pattern that produces the clearest evidence of progress.

faqs.question: Will a maths tutor travel to our building in Deira?
faqs.answer: Not from us. All UAE lessons are online, one-to-one, over live video on a shared whiteboard, and IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that is part of our India service. For mathematics the whiteboard is a genuine advantage: both people write, the student's working is preserved rather than erased, and the board is saved between sessions. In-home tutoring exists in the Dubai market at AED 180 to 500 an hour including travel for families who need that format.

faqs.question: How many sessions does it take to move a maths grade?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on what is wrong, which is why the first session should be diagnostic. A narrow missed topic such as scale factors or frequency density is one or two sessions. A method-mark habit is two to four weeks of layout drilling. A weak algebraic base is a term of weekly work, because it is the base everything else rests on. Problem solving across topics needs fortnightly full papers across a term. Anyone quoting a session count before seeing a marked paper is guessing.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-deira.closingHeading: Send the code, the tier and the last marked paper
dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-deira.closingBody: Those three things answer every question on this page. The code tells us which past papers are useful. The tier tells us what is available to be won. The marked paper tells us whether the problem is content, method, timing or a weak algebraic base, and those need four different plans. Add whether a fourth mathematics paper is on the timetable and where your child is heading at 16, and the plan can look past the next assessment. The first lesson is free, before any payment. Lessons are online, one-to-one, over live video on a shared whiteboard, in Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-difc.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IGCSE Mathematics one-to-one over live video. Each works to a single specification and tier, and each builds a contact pattern around the student's real school end time rather than fitting them into a standard weekly slot.

intro.heading: Mathematics is a frequency problem, and the school run sets the frequency
paragraphs: Most tutoring advice treats every subject the same way: find a tutor, book an hour, repeat weekly. For IGCSE mathematics that is close to the worst available pattern, and for a family in a DIFC tower it is also the pattern the school run most obstructs. Mathematics is a fluency subject. Technique that is not used decays between sittings in a way that historical case-study knowledge does not, which means four short contacts a week produce more than one long one, and a session that falls on the same evening as the maths homework is worth more than one that falls three days later.

DIFC's particular situation is that no school sits inside the district. Every IGCSE candidate here travels out, most often west to the Al Safa and Jumeirah cluster, or across to Sobha Hartland, Al Jaddaf, Al Quoz and Al Barsha. The return journey sets the earliest hour a session can begin, and it varies by thirty to fifty minutes depending on the campus and on whether the child takes a bus or a car. A maths pattern designed without that information is a pattern that will be late by ten minutes most weeks and will quietly stop being taken seriously.

So this page builds the maths plan from the day outwards. It covers which session shapes actually fit a DIFC week, how the school's own maths timetable should determine which evening the session falls on, what a set change means and when it can happen, why the twenty-minute daily habit outperforms the weekly hour, and how the non-calculator and calculator papers need different slots in the week. The mathematics content is here, inside that structure, because content without a workable schedule attached is the thing most families already have.

Two facts anchor the calendar. A UAE candidate sits the June series or the November series: Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level examinations in a June series and a November series, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May/June and November each year. And the Cambridge February/March series is offered to India only, so a plan built around a February or March exam window is built on the wrong country's calendar.

On delivery, plainly. IB Gram teaches UAE families one-to-one over live video. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE and we operate no centre here; home visiting is a service we run only in India. For a frequency-based maths pattern this is close to a requirement rather than a preference: two or three short contacts a week are logistically impossible if somebody has to drive across central Dubai for each one, and they are straightforward over video. Every market rate quoted below belongs to the provider that published it, with the month it was read, and none of them is a price of ours.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-difc.programmesIntro: The right contact pattern changes with the year group, because what mathematics demands changes. These are the stages in play for a DIFC family, framed by the rhythm each one needs.

programmes.name: Year 10, building the habit
programmes.description: The year to establish a rhythm rather than to fix a crisis. One weekly contact plus a short daily practice habit means content is consolidated as it is taught, which prevents the compounding that makes Year 11 expensive. It is also the year in which the tier entry decision is made, so the work doubles as the evidence that conversation will need.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the tier entry decision is usually made during Year 10 or very early Year 11, within the board's deadlines, on the basis of internal assessment. For a DIFC family, Year 10 evenings are long enough to carry a pattern and Year 11 evenings are not, which is the practical argument for starting earlier.

programmes.name: Year 11, protecting the rhythm
programmes.description: Nine or ten subjects competing for roughly three usable evening hours. Mathematics suffers in this environment because it is the subject that penalises gaps most, and because other subjects set work that feels more urgent. The useful pattern here is short and frequent rather than long and occasional, with the session anchored to the maths homework evening.
programmes.countryNote: A DIFC student arriving home around 4pm has the freshest hour of the evening available, which is the one most families waste. The short westward school run makes a 4pm maths contact achievable here where most of the emirate cannot start before 5pm, and the 5pm to 7pm window is contested city-wide.

programmes.name: Year 9 and the set you land in
programmes.description: The year that quietly decides the next two, because the maths set a student is in at the end of Year 9 heavily influences the tier they are entered for. Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests give an external datapoint before that decision. A Year 9 in a lower set with a year to work has genuine options; a Year 11 in a lower set in the spring term has very few.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The October window gives a Dubai family evidence before the set and tier decisions rather than after them, which is when most DIFC parents first hear the word Core.

programmes.name: What the IGCSE maths grade opens
programmes.description: Extended tier Cambridge 0580 or Higher tier Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 is the realistic prerequisite for IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and for most A Level mathematics courses. A Core or Foundation tier grade closes those routes regardless of how strong the grade itself is, which makes the tier a sixth-form decision taken two years early.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places. A wider sixth-form choice makes the Year 11 maths tier more consequential, because more doors exist to be closed by it.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-difc.subjectsIntro: The topic strands of IGCSE Mathematics, annotated with the contact pattern each one actually needs. Some want frequent short practice, others want a single long explanation followed by homework, and treating them identically is why many plans underperform.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The clearest case for frequency. Factorising, rearranging and algebraic fractions decay fastest between sittings and underpin almost every other strand. Fifteen minutes four times a week beats an hour once. It is also the strand whose weakness silently caps performance in graphs, trigonometry and the harder geometry questions.

subjects.name: Number, ratio and percentages
subjects.description: Mostly technique, so one good explanation plus repeated homework works well. Reverse percentages are the standout: students apply the forward operation and lose the marks, and two sessions make the correct approach automatic. Bounds and standard form are similar, quick and reliable to repair.

subjects.name: Graphs and functions
subjects.description: Needs a long explanation then practice, rather than frequent short contact. Marks are lost on the written justification rather than the sketch: a correct transformation without the stated mapping scores nothing for the algebra. This is a one-session-then-homework strand.

subjects.name: Trigonometry and Pythagoras
subjects.description: Benefits from frequency because the sine and cosine rules are recalled rather than derived under pressure. The three-dimensional questions need a single taught method for identifying the right triangle inside a solid, then repetition until it is automatic.

subjects.name: Mensuration and circle theorems
subjects.description: Circle theorems are memorisation with a reasoning requirement attached: naming the theorem earns the mark. A flashcard habit between sessions does most of the work, which makes this the cheapest strand in contact time and one of the most reliable in marks.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.description: One long explanation suits this strand better than frequent contact, with the exception of histograms with unequal class widths. Frequency density is a definition students half-remember and then guess at, and it needs explicit repetition rather than a single explanation.

subjects.name: Vectors and transformations
subjects.description: The proof-style vector questions appear late in Higher papers and are frequently left blank by students who could do them, because they have never practised the layout of a vector argument. One taught layout plus three worked examples usually makes the whole question type accessible.

subjects.name: Non-calculator fluency
subjects.levels: Where the specification sets a calculator-free paper
subjects.description: Fraction arithmetic, surds, index laws and estimation by hand. The purest frequency strand in the subject: it rebuilds through short daily practice and does not rebuild through weekly explanation. It also needs its own slot, because mixing it with calculator work in one session teaches neither.

subjects.name: Calculator technique
subjects.description: Using the device as a mathematical tool rather than an arithmetic one, with bracket discipline and awareness of premature rounding inside multi-step calculations. Low contact time, high return, and almost never the thing a family thinks they are buying.

subjects.name: Past-paper discipline
subjects.description: Whole papers worked to time and marked against the published scheme, with losses coded by question type. This needs a long uninterrupted slot, which a weeknight after a DIFC commute cannot provide. It belongs on a weekend morning or in a school break.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: A genuine extra subject in a week that is already full. Worth taking on only where the main specification is secure, and worth scheduling as a separate contact rather than folded into the main maths session, where it tends to crowd out consolidation.

subjects.name: Formula recall
subjects.description: Which formulae are printed on the paper and which must be recalled differs by board and by tier, and students routinely memorise the provided list while neglecting the required one. A homework task rather than a session task, but it needs to be set from the correct specification document.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-difc.regionsTitle: The campuses DIFC maths candidates attend, and what each does to the pattern

sections.heading: Why two short contacts beat one long session in mathematics
paragraphs: Mathematics is unusual among IGCSE subjects in how quickly unused technique becomes unavailable. A student who factorises confidently on Monday and does not factorise again until the following Monday has lost part of that confidence, not because they have forgotten the method but because the retrieval has become slow, and slow retrieval under exam timing reads as not knowing. History case-study knowledge does not behave this way. Algebra does.

The practical consequence is that the familiar weekly hour is a poor shape for this subject. Two forty-minute contacts on separate evenings deliver the same paid minutes and considerably more retention, because the second contact retrieves what the first one built while it is still retrievable. Three twenty-five-minute contacts would be better again for pure fluency work, though at that length a session struggles to also diagnose or teach anything new.

There is a second reason the split pattern wins in a DIFC week, which is attention. An eighty-minute mathematics session with a Year 11 who arrived home at 4.30pm after a day at school in Al Quoz is productive for perhaps fifty of those minutes. Two forty-minute contacts are productive for close to eighty. The parent pays for the same hours and the child receives noticeably more of them.

The reason this pattern is rare in Dubai is logistical rather than pedagogical. Nobody drives across central Dubai twice a week to teach forty minutes, so in-home providers do not offer it and centre timetables cannot accommodate it. Over video it is trivial. That is a genuine structural advantage of online delivery for mathematics specifically, and it is the main reason this page recommends the pattern rather than the format.

sections.heading: Put the session on the maths homework evening
paragraphs: A detail nobody mentions and that costs nothing to get right: which evening the session falls on matters almost as much as what happens in it. A Dubai Year 11 typically has four or five mathematics lessons a week, with homework set after some of them. A tutoring contact that lands on the evening maths homework is due is doing two jobs at once, because the student brings a specific, current, graded piece of work to it. A contact three days later is doing one job, in the abstract.

This is worth a direct question to your child rather than to the school: which days do you have maths, and which day is the homework usually due? Two minutes of conversation, and the answer frequently reveals that the existing session is on the worst possible evening. Families often choose a slot for adult-calendar reasons and then wonder why the session feels disconnected from school.

Where two contacts a week are possible, the better arrangement is one on the homework evening and one on the evening before the next maths lesson, so the student arrives in class having retrieved the technique rather than having last seen it four days earlier. Teachers notice this and it affects how a student is perceived in class, which in turn affects set placement, which is not a trivial downstream effect.

One caution specific to this corridor. If your child schools towards Al Barsha or Al Quoz, Sunday and Thursday evenings are the heaviest on those routes and a slot on either day will be the one that slips most often. A pattern that is theoretically correct and practically late every week is worse than a slightly less optimal pattern that happens on time. Choose the evening the journey supports, then optimise within that.

sections.heading: Sets, set changes and the window a parent can actually use
paragraphs: In most Dubai British-curriculum schools, mathematics is set by ability from Year 7 onwards, and the set a student is in at the end of Year 9 heavily influences the IGCSE tier they are entered for. This is the mechanism by which a decision taken quietly at thirteen limits a sixth-form choice at sixteen, and almost no tutoring page in this market explains it.

Set changes happen, but they happen on the school's schedule and on the school's evidence. Typically they follow an internal assessment point, which is usually the end of a term or a reporting cycle. That means the useful window for intervention opens roughly six to eight weeks before an assessment point, not when a parent first becomes concerned. A family that understands this stops asking for a set change and starts asking what evidence would support one, which is a much more productive conversation.

The evidence that moves a set is internal assessment performance, which means the right work is not general confidence-building but targeted preparation for the specific assessments the school uses to make the decision. Ask the head of mathematics, in writing, when the next set review is, what evidence it considers, and what performance would support a move. Schools answer this question when it is asked clearly, and many parents never ask it.

What a parent should not do is treat a set change as the goal in itself. Sometimes a student in a lower set with excellent teaching and a secure grade within the tier is in the right place, and the honest advice is to maximise the grade available rather than chase a move that would leave them struggling. The tier matters because of what it opens at sixteen, so the real question is which sixth-form routes the family needs kept open, and then whether the tier delivers them.

sections.heading: Twenty minutes a day, marked before the next contact
paragraphs: The single highest-return habit in IGCSE mathematics costs nothing and almost nobody sustains it. Twenty minutes of mixed practice on four days a week, covering strands taught weeks ago rather than only the current topic, builds the retrieval speed that exam timing demands. One weekly hour cannot build it, because retrieval speed comes from spacing rather than from duration.

The reason families do not sustain it is not laziness but feedback. Twenty minutes of practice that nobody looks at produces no visible progress, so it stops within a fortnight. Twenty minutes that is marked and discussed at the next contact produces visible progress, so it continues. That is the actual function of a weekly session in a well-designed maths plan: it sets the practice, marks it, and makes the daily habit survivable.

The practice should be mixed rather than blocked. Twenty questions on the current topic feels productive and builds very little retrieval strength, because the student knows what method is required before reading the question. Twenty questions drawn from six different strands is harder, feels worse, and is substantially more useful, because selecting the method is the skill the exam actually tests. A good tutor builds the mixed set; a parent can also build it from past papers the school provides.

For a DIFC Year 11, the practical placement is the twenty minutes immediately after arriving home, before any longer homework begins. At 4pm or 4.30pm a student is tired from travel but not yet from work, and twenty minutes is short enough to be tolerable at that moment. Pushed to 8.30pm, after two hours of other subjects, the same twenty minutes produces very little and generates a nightly argument.

sections.heading: Two papers, two different slots in the week
paragraphs: Most IGCSE mathematics specifications set one paper where a calculator is not permitted and one where it is, and the two need genuinely different preparation. Mixing them in a single session teaches neither well, because the habits conflict: one rewards by-hand fluency and estimation, the other rewards device technique and rounding discipline.

Non-calculator work belongs in the short, early, frequent contacts. It is fluency, it decays fastest, and it responds to spacing. Fraction arithmetic, surds, index laws and mental estimation are exactly the material a twenty-minute slot handles well. A student who has revised entirely with a calculator is unprepared for the paper that does not allow one, and the deficit is in arithmetic confidence rather than in mathematics, which means it is fixable but only if it is identified.

Calculator work belongs in the longer slot, usually the weekend morning, because the useful practice is whole questions and whole papers where premature rounding inside a multi-step calculation is the thing being hunted. Answers must be given to the accuracy the specification requires, and a correct method with an over-rounded final answer loses the accuracy mark with the mathematics entirely right. That is a per-question discipline best built across a full paper rather than in fragments.

Which papers are calculator-free, and which formulae are printed rather than recalled, differs by specification and by tier. Confirm both against the specification document the school holds, because boards revise them and students routinely memorise the provided list while neglecting the required one. No tutoring page, this one included, should be the source of record for that detail.
bullets: Non-calculator fluency belongs in short, frequent, early contacts

sections.heading: Confirm the specification before the pattern is set
paragraphs: A perfectly designed contact pattern aimed at the wrong specification is a wasted term. The schools DIFC families use are split between Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580, with Core and Extended tiers, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics Specification A 4MA1, with Foundation and Higher tiers. The content overlaps heavily; the phrasing, paper structures and formula provision do not.

Email the school's examinations officer and ask in writing for the exact specification code and the tier of entry. Both answers arrive within a reply or two. A notable number of DIFC families discover at this point that they had assumed a board, usually from an older sibling or from a school in another country. Working the wrong board's papers is one of the most complete wastes available in this purchase, because every contact in the plan is then pointed slightly wrong.

Also confirm the Cambridge examination zone if your child sits Cambridge papers. Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and states that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone timetable. Build the revision calendar from the timetable your own examinations officer confirms, never from a version found online.

Dates in the past are safe to state because they are checkable, and they show the shape of a series better than any projection. Pearson's November 2026 final International GCSE timetable ran to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026. November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, which is why a plan should link the live official timetable rather than restating dates that can be revised.

sections.heading: What the pattern costs, counted per contact
paragraphs: A frequency-based plan changes how the published rates read, because the useful unit becomes the contact rather than the hour. Two forty-minute contacts a week is eighty paid minutes, so a plan quoted per hour needs converting before it can be compared with a single weekly session.

The published Dubai bands, each attributed to the provider or publication that stated it and read in October 2026: Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 at the budget end of online tutoring. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 online. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 and IB, IGCSE and A-Level specialist work at AED 200 to 450 or more, with independent home tutors reaching AED 200 to 500 once travel is priced in. TutorChase quotes AED 270 and BartyED AED 650 at the premium end. Monthly packages include AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Note what those monthly in-home packages imply about frequency: four two-hour sessions a month is one long session a week, which is the pattern mathematics responds to least well. The package shape is driven by the economics of travel rather than by what the subject needs, and a family buying it is buying a schedule designed around somebody's drive. The AED 799 online package of eight sessions a month, by contrast, is two contacts a week, which is the right shape whoever provides it.

IB Gram does not publish a UAE rate card on these pages and does not present any of these figures as ours. The free trial lesson exists so a family can see the teaching before discussing money, and it should be taken at the hour and on the evening you actually intend to use, so the pattern is tested along with the tutor. For wider budget context, KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion.

sections.heading: Breaks, Ramadan and the decay nobody plans for
paragraphs: Mathematics loses more over a school break than any other IGCSE subject, for the same reason it benefits most from frequency. Three weeks without retrieval and the fluency is noticeably slower on return, even though no knowledge has been lost. Families notice this as a bad first week back and attribute it to attitude.

The fix is small and specific. Twenty minutes of mixed practice on three days a week through a break preserves almost all of the fluency, and that is a fraction of the time a family would spend on catch-up afterwards. It does not require a tutor present; it requires a set of mixed questions and somebody looking at the answers. A session at the start and end of a break brackets it usefully.

Breaks are also the right window for the thing that cannot fit a weeknight: a full paper under timed conditions, marked against the published scheme with losses coded by question type. Two of those across a one-week break are worth more than six rushed term-time sessions, and they produce the diagnostic data that shapes the next term. New content taught during a break tends not to survive the return, because nothing reinforces it for a fortnight.

Ramadan needs its own plan rather than improvisation. School days shorten, evening routines reorganise around iftar, and the usual 5pm slot stops working for most DIFC families. Early-afternoon contacts and post-iftar contacts both work, and for a frequency-based maths plan the short-contact pattern actually survives Ramadan better than a long weekly session does, because a twenty-five-minute contact fits into a reorganised evening where ninety minutes does not. Agree the pattern before the month begins.

sections.heading: Regulation, honesty and starting from DIFC
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit, and it is checkable. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 Regarding the Introduction of Private Tuition Work Permits. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. MoHRE's own service page lists no fees and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount appears here.

One boundary worth knowing before anybody suggests the obvious shortcut. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Verify the exact current wording against ADEK's own policy document, since this is press-reported. Beyond compliance, hiring the teacher who sets your child's internal assessments removes the independent second opinion that is half of what tutoring buys.

On equivalency, the sourced British-track rule is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or above or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the five. At least one ranking site in this market publishes six subjects, which is wrong. IB Gram does not perform, submit or guarantee equivalency for anybody, and tutoring is not a requirement for equivalency, admission or progression.

And the claims we decline. IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, Ministry of Education, MoHRE, IB or Cambridge accreditation, licence, approval or partnership, and has no office, branch or centre in the UAE. We do not publish any self-asserted rating or review count, do not describe tutors as examiners without evidence of current status, and do not write, complete or edit assessed work. To start, bring the specification code, the tier, the days your child has maths, and the two most recent marked papers, and the pattern designs itself in one conversation.

faqs.question: Is one weekly maths hour enough, or should we split it?
faqs.answer: For mathematics specifically, splitting usually wins. Two forty-minute contacts on separate evenings deliver the same paid minutes and more retention, because the second retrieves what the first built while it is still retrievable. There is an attention argument too: an eighty-minute session with a Year 11 who arrived home at 4.30pm is productive for perhaps fifty minutes, where two forty-minute contacts are productive for close to eighty. The pattern is only practical over video, which is why in-home and centre providers rarely offer it.

faqs.question: Which evening should my child's maths session fall on?
faqs.answer: The evening maths homework is due. A Dubai Year 11 typically has four or five mathematics lessons a week with homework after some of them, and a contact that lands on the homework evening has a specific, current, graded piece of work to use. A contact three days later works in the abstract. Ask your child which days they have maths and when homework is due, then build around that. Many families choose a slot for adult-calendar reasons and never revisit it.

faqs.question: What does twenty minutes of daily maths practice actually achieve?
faqs.answer: It builds retrieval speed, which is what exam timing tests and what a weekly hour cannot produce. Twenty minutes on four days, drawn from six different strands rather than only the current topic, is harder than it sounds and considerably more useful, because selecting the method is the real skill. The reason families abandon it is feedback: unmarked practice produces no visible progress and stops within a fortnight. Practice that is marked and discussed at the next contact continues, which is a large part of what a weekly session is actually for.

faqs.question: Why does blocked practice on one topic feel better and work worse?
faqs.answer: Because the student knows which method is required before reading the question, so no selection is happening. Twenty questions on circle theorems feels productive and builds very little of the skill a paper tests, where any question could be any strand. Mixed practice across six strands feels worse, produces more errors, and builds the retrieval and selection the examination actually measures. A tutor should be building the mixed set; a parent can also build it from past papers the school provides.

faqs.question: How does my child's maths set affect the tier they are entered for?
faqs.answer: Heavily. In most Dubai British-curriculum schools mathematics is set by ability from Year 7, and the set at the end of Year 9 strongly influences the IGCSE tier of entry. That is how a decision taken quietly at thirteen limits a sixth-form choice at sixteen, since Extended or Higher tier is the realistic prerequisite for IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level and for most A Level mathematics. Ask the school in writing which set your child is in and how the tier decision will be made.

faqs.question: When can a Dubai school actually move my child up a maths set?
faqs.answer: Set changes follow the school's internal assessment points, usually the end of a term or a reporting cycle, rather than following a parent's concern. That means the useful intervention window opens roughly six to eight weeks before an assessment point. The productive question to the head of mathematics is not for a move but what evidence would support one, and when the next review is. Schools answer that clearly when it is asked clearly, and a surprising number of parents never ask it.

faqs.question: Should chasing a higher maths set always be the goal?
faqs.answer: No. A student in a lower set with strong teaching and a secure grade within the tier may be in the right place, and the honest advice is sometimes to maximise the grade available rather than to chase a move that would leave them struggling. The real question is which sixth-form routes you need kept open, and whether the tier delivers them. Extended or Higher tier keeps IB Higher Level and A Level mathematics open; Core or Foundation generally does not, regardless of how good the grade is.

faqs.question: Why do the calculator and non-calculator papers need separate sessions?
faqs.answer: Because the habits conflict. Non-calculator work rewards by-hand fluency and estimation, which decays fastest and rebuilds through short frequent practice, so it belongs in the early short contacts. Calculator papers reward device technique and rounding discipline, where premature rounding inside a multi-step calculation is the thing being hunted, and that is best built across whole questions and whole papers in a longer slot. Mixing both in one session teaches neither properly. Confirm which paper is calculator-free from the specification document the school holds.

faqs.question: How much maths fluency does my child lose over a school break?
faqs.answer: Enough to be noticeable, and more than in any other IGCSE subject. Three weeks without retrieval leaves the fluency slower on return even though no knowledge has been lost, which families usually read as a bad attitude in the first week back. Twenty minutes of mixed practice on three days a week through a break preserves nearly all of it, for a fraction of the time the subsequent catch-up would take. A contact at the start and end of the break brackets it usefully.

faqs.question: Is a school break a good time for an intensive maths push?
faqs.answer: It is the right time for whole timed papers and the wrong time for new content. A break is the only period a student has uninterrupted days, which is exactly what a full paper under examination conditions requires and exactly what a weeknight after a DIFC commute cannot provide. Two properly marked papers across a one-week break produce the diagnostic data that shapes the next term. New topics taught in a break tend not to survive the return, because nothing reinforces them for a fortnight.

faqs.question: Does a short-contact maths pattern survive Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Better than a long weekly session does, which is a useful side effect. School days shorten and evening routines reorganise around iftar, so a ninety-minute slot often becomes impossible where a twenty-five or forty-minute contact still fits, either in the early afternoon or after iftar. The thing that fails is improvisation: deciding week by week typically costs three or four weeks at a point in the year when weeks are expensive. Agree the alternative pattern before the month begins rather than during it.

faqs.question: Which specification is my child sitting, and why does it change the plan?
faqs.answer: Email the examinations officer for the exact code. In Dubai it is usually Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580, tiered Core and Extended, or Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics Specification A 4MA1, tiered Foundation and Higher. The content overlaps heavily but the phrasing, paper structures and formula provision do not. In a plan built on frequency, every contact is pointed at the papers, so pointing them at the wrong board's papers wastes all of them rather than some of them.

faqs.question: Which maths formulae are printed on the paper and which must be learned?
faqs.answer: That differs by specification and by tier, and it is worth checking rather than assuming. Students routinely memorise the formulae that are provided and neglect the ones that are not, which is a pure loss of marks created by a misunderstanding. Ask the school for the specification document and read the formula provision section, or ask the mathematics teacher for the recall list directly. No tutoring website should be your source of record for that, because boards revise it and a wrong list costs marks on the day.

faqs.question: What does a two-contact-a-week maths plan cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Convert published hourly rates into the pattern. Two forty-minute contacts is eighty paid minutes a week. At the budget online bands, Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 online, and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table places specialist work at AED 200 to 450 or more. The AED 799 monthly package for eight online sessions is already two contacts a week. Those are each provider's own published figures read in October 2026, not IB Gram prices.

faqs.question: Why are in-home monthly packages always four long sessions?
faqs.answer: Because the economics of travel shape the package rather than the needs of the subject. Published in-home packages in this market run AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour sessions, which is one long session a week: the pattern mathematics responds to least well. A provider cannot profitably drive across central Dubai twice a week for forty minutes, so the offer becomes fewer, longer visits. A family buying it is buying a schedule designed around a journey, and for maths that is the wrong shape.

faqs.question: Can a maths tutor visit our DIFC apartment twice a week?
faqs.answer: Not from us, and in practice not from anyone at a sensible price. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the United Arab Emirates and has no office, branch or tuition centre here; home visiting is a service we run only in India. All UAE tuition is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. The relevant point is that the frequency mathematics needs is only economic over video: two short contacts a week is straightforward online and close to impossible as a pair of drives across central Dubai in the evening peak.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-difc.closingHeading: Fix the pattern before you book the tutor
dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-difc.closingBody: Four free pieces of information produce a maths plan that will survive a term. Which days your child has mathematics and when the homework is due. The actual arrival home, measured across five days rather than estimated. The exact specification code and tier, confirmed in writing by the school. And the two most recent marked papers rather than the grades. With those, the evening, the hour, the pattern and the content are all decided by evidence. Bring them to a short consultation on Gulf Standard Time and take the free trial in the slot you actually intend to use, so the pattern is tested alongside the teaching. No card is required, and the session ends with a written note of the marks being lost and the practice set for the week ahead.

intro.heading: Four comparisons, and one that does not matter
paragraphs: Parents in this corridor spend a lot of energy on the wrong comparison. The conversation in building groups and at school gates is usually about which community has better access to tutors, with Discovery Gardens families assuming the villa side has the advantage. Discovery Gardens is a high-density apartment community of 291 buildings in themed districts beside Ibn Battuta; Al Furjan next door is villas and townhouses. The housing differs and the mathematics does not.

The comparisons that do decide an IGCSE mathematics grade are four, and all four are answerable from documents the school already holds. Which board and syllabus code your child is entered for: Cambridge 0580 or Pearson Edexcel 4MA1. Which tier: Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher. Whether the entry includes a paper sat without a calculator. And whether revision consists of marked papers or unmarked topic work.

Each of those has a right answer for your child and each is commonly got wrong. Boards are assumed rather than checked, and several schools in this corridor enter different boards in different departments. Tiers are noticed as a notification rather than discussed as a decision. The non-calculator paper is prepared for in the last month rather than maintained for two years. And revision almost always means topic work, because that is what a syllabus list invites.

This page works through all four, with a table for each of the first three, and then explains why the neighbourhood comparison is a distraction. It also compares the realistic sources of help in this corridor, from the school's own clinic to a centre class near Ibn Battuta to one-to-one, because the right tool depends entirely on what the diagnosis says.

IB Gram's own position is stated plainly rather than argued for. We match on the syllabus code and tier from your child's entry list, name the tutor before the first lesson, and deliver every UAE session one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time between 15:30 and 21:30. No tutor attends a UAE address; home visiting is a service we run only in India.

For mathematics in an apartment that last point is less of a limitation than it sounds. A session is shared written working: the student writes, the tutor sees it, and both annotate the same page. What that needs is a desk, over-ear headphones and the marked work to hand, rather than a room with a door, which is the one resource a two-bedroom flat in this community does not have spare.

One timing note before the comparisons themselves. Three of the four are decided in Year 10 rather than Year 11: the board is fixed at entry, the tier closes with the entry window months before the papers, and the non-calculator habit has to be maintained rather than rebuilt. Only the revision-method comparison is still fully open in the final year, which is why families who engage in Year 10 get decisions and families who engage in Year 11 get information.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3 mathematics, Years 7 to 9

programmes.name: IGCSE Mathematics, Years 10 to 11
programmes.description: Two years ending in terminal written papers, with board and tier fixed at entry. Cambridge 0580 runs Core and Extended; Pearson 4MA1 runs Foundation and Higher. The dominant loss across both is method marks, since working is credited independently of the answer, which is why topic revision so often produces no movement.

Students travel out of the community for school and are home from about 15:50 on the nearest routes or 16:30 from the Al Barsha corridor, so a 17:00 or 17:30 start is normal. Calculus, logarithms, series and trigonometric identities arrive a year early, which makes the first post-16 term revision rather than new content. It is examined in its own right rather than being enrichment.

programmes.description: Both routes usually require grade 6 or 7 and both move considerably faster than Year 11. Advanced Level expects algebraic fluency from week one; IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches expects that plus early proof. A Core or Foundation entry frequently closes both, which is the long shadow the tier comparison casts.
programmes.countryNote: Families here commonly change schools at 16, because full IB Diploma provision in this corridor is thinner than further north. A summer bridging block therefore does double duty: it closes the mathematical gap and removes one unfamiliar variable from a term that already includes a new school.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-discovery-gar.subjectsIntro: IGCSE mathematics is one qualification and a dozen separable skills. Each note names where marks go when that area is weak.

subjects.name: Number, bounds and accuracy
subjects.description: Standard form, ratio, percentage change and upper and lower bounds. Bounds questions are lost to reading rather than to method: students treat them as a topic to memorise instead of a rule about measurement, and miss the accuracy demand written into the question.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation
subjects.description: Expanding, factorising, rearranging and solving. The commonest source of lost marks on the whole paper, because almost every other topic routes through it. Negatives and fractions inside one expression is where fluency breaks, and that is a drilling problem rather than a teaching one.

subjects.name: Equations and inequalities
subjects.description: Linear, simultaneous and quadratic equations, with the formula and completing the square at the upper tier. Students abandon method once a calculator produces a root, forfeiting the working marks that carry most of the question's value.

subjects.name: Coordinate geometry and graphs
subjects.description: Gradients, midpoints, parallel and perpendicular lines, and curve sketching. Reading a gradient from two plotted points instead of from the line of best fit is a mark-scheme error that appears in mathematics and science papers alike, and one session fixes it for good.

subjects.name: Functions and transformations
subjects.description: Function notation, composite and inverse functions, and graph transformations. Notation is the barrier rather than concept: students who decode notation each time it appears run out of time on papers they could otherwise finish comfortably.

subjects.name: Geometry and angle reasoning
subjects.description: Circle theorems, polygon angles, congruence and similarity. Marks go to the stated reason as much as to the angle, so an unstated theorem loses half the credit even with a correct value. Writing the reason is a habit worth drilling in Year 10.

subjects.name: Mensuration
subjects.description: Area, volume, surface area, arcs and sectors. Multi-step by nature, and compound shapes need decomposing before any calculation. Students who start calculating before planning lose both accuracy and time, which compounds on a tight paper.

subjects.name: Trigonometry
subjects.description: Right-angled trigonometry, sine and cosine rules, bearings and three-dimensional problems. Bearings questions are lost on the diagram rather than the calculation, and three-dimensional questions on failing to identify the relevant triangle before starting.

subjects.name: Vectors and set notation
subjects.description: Column vectors, magnitude and geometric reasoning, plus set notation in probability. Short, mark-dense and routinely skipped in revision because they look unfamiliar. For a student in the final term they are usually the fastest available marks on the paper.

subjects.name: Probability
subjects.description: Tree diagrams and conditional probability. The diagram does most of the work, so students who draw it carefully rarely lose marks and students who attempt it mentally rarely keep them. Set notation here is examined and frequently untaught.

subjects.name: Statistics and data handling
subjects.description: Cumulative frequency, histograms with unequal class widths, box plots and averages from grouped data. Frequency density is the single most reliably lost idea in the data section, skipped in class about as often as it is examined.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Calculus, logarithms, series and trigonometric identities alongside the main entry. The best bridge into post-16 mathematics available at 16, and the hardest subject in this list to find local provision for in any model in this corridor.

sections.heading: Comparison one: Cambridge 0580 against Pearson 4MA1
paragraphs: This is the comparison that costs most when it is skipped, and it is settled by one free document. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics is syllabus 0580 with Core and Extended tiers. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A is 4MA1 with Foundation and Higher tiers. Both are credible qualifications of similar standing and they are not interchangeable in any respect that matters to revision.

The differences run through the whole preparation. The number of papers differs. Calculator provision across papers differs. The formula support given in the exam room differs, so students must know what they will and will not be handed. Mark-scheme conventions differ in how method is credited. And grade boundaries are published separately, so comparing a raw mark against the wrong board's boundaries is meaningless.

The failure this produces is slow and invisible. A competent tutor works from the other board's past papers, teaching correct mathematics with the wrong conventions and the wrong paper structure. Topics are covered, command phrasing is unfamiliar, and nobody notices until the mock. In a terminal-exam subject that is a term of revision aimed slightly off target, which no amount of effort inside the term recovers.

Tier naming adds a second layer of confusion. A parent told their child is on Higher tier may assume that is the ceiling; in Cambridge terms the equivalent is Extended. Conversely Core and Foundation sound milder than they are, since both cap the grade. Ask for the entry list and read three things from it: the board, the code, and the tier. It takes one email to the exams officer.

sections.heading: Comparison two: the lower tier against the upper tier
paragraphs: The tier comparison has the longest consequences of anything on this page and it is usually presented to parents as a decision already made. Core and Foundation entries cap the grade available. Extended and Higher reach the full range. Most British-curriculum schools want grade 6 or 7 in a subject before accepting it at Advanced Level, and IB Diploma Higher Level entry usually asks the same, so a capped entry can close a post-16 route.

Schools generally recommend on the evidence of Year 10 performance and are usually right. Where a parent can add something is in understanding what the evidence says rather than disputing the conclusion. Three marked papers answer it. If losses are content, the gap is closable within a term. If they are method and reading, the student is stronger than the mark suggests. If algebraic fluency itself is missing, the lower tier protects the grade.

That last case deserves saying honestly, because it is the one no tutor benefits from saying. A student pushed to the upper tier on ambition can score below what they would have achieved on the lower paper, since the questions assume fluency they do not have and time pressure compounds it. A grade kept at the lower tier is worth more than a grade lost at the higher one for most purposes.

The timing is the whole point of this comparison. Everything above is a Year 10 conversation. By the spring of Year 11 the entry window has closed and the only remaining variable is performance on a paper already chosen. Families in this community who book a weekly session in Year 10 get this conversation while it is still a decision; those who book in Year 11 receive it as information.

sections.heading: Comparison three: the calculator paper against the one without
paragraphs: Where an entry includes a paper sat without a calculator, that paper examines a different skill from the rest of the qualification and it needs its own preparation across two years rather than four weeks. Manual arithmetic, fractions, surds and paper-based algebraic manipulation all erode quietly through two years of calculator-assisted homework, and the erosion is invisible until a paper removes the calculator.

The remedy is maintenance rather than revision, and the difference matters financially. Ten minutes of manual work inside every weekly session across two years holds the fluency at almost no marginal cost. Rebuilding it in the final six weeks is possible and expensive, because fluency responds to frequency and there is no frequency left by then. This is the main argument for starting mathematics support in Year 10 rather than Year 11.

The calculator paper has its own discipline, which students treat as unnecessary. Marks are available for working even when technology produced the answer, so the habit to build is writing what was entered and what came back. A bare number shows no method, and in multi-step questions the method carries most of the value. Knowing the specific model's menus also saves real time under pressure.

For a Discovery Gardens family there is a practical note attached. Find out which calculator model the school requires and work on that one, because statistical and table functions differ between models in ways that cost time and invite misread outputs. It is a five-minute question at the start of an arrangement and it protects marks in the exam room two years later.

sections.heading: Comparison four: marked papers against topic revision
paragraphs: This is the comparison most families never consciously make, because topic revision is the default. A syllabus list invites it, schools often set it, and it feels productive: the student works through a topic, answers questions, and ticks it off. What it does not produce is information about why marks are being lost, which is the only thing a revision plan should be built from.

The alternative is marked paper work and it has four steps. The paper is attempted under timed conditions in one sitting without notes. It is marked against the actual mark scheme, strictly, with method and accuracy marks separated. Every loss is categorised by cause: method not shown, notation, arithmetic, misread question, topic gap or ran out of time. Then the two largest categories are targeted before the next paper.

The categorisation is the whole value. A student losing nine marks across a paper has two causes rather than nine problems, and the two causes point to completely different work. Six marks lost to method not shown and three to timing is nothing like six lost to a topic gap and three to notation. Students cannot usually do this alone, because they see the question they got wrong rather than the behaviour that caused it.

An error log is the cheap extension: three columns recording the paper, the loss type and one sentence on what to do differently. After four papers the pattern is undeniable and revision stops being a matter of opinion about which topics feel weak. It takes about five minutes per paper, it costs nothing, and in our experience almost no student does it without being asked.

sections.heading: The comparison that does not matter: which community you live in
paragraphs: Having given three tables to comparisons that count, the neighbourhood one deserves a direct answer. Discovery Gardens and Al Furjan draw on exactly the same pool of mathematics tutors, because neither community has a resident population of subject specialists and both are reached on the same drive from the Al Barsha and Jumeirah areas where Dubai's tutors actually live and work. Visiting tutors quote them in the same band.

What genuinely differs is study space, and it runs against Discovery Gardens. A villa usually offers a room with a door; most flats here do not, and the realistic setup is a desk in a shared living area. That is a real difference and it has a practical answer: over-ear headphones with a microphone, plus a household agreement that the hour is a timetabled lesson rather than homework.

Travel actually runs the other way. Discovery Gardens is compact, so pickup and drop-off is quicker than the long bus loops that spread Al Furjan arrival times across fifty minutes for the same school. A Discovery Gardens student on a Dubai Investments Park route can be home by 15:50, which gives a slightly longer usable evening than the equivalent villa family gets.

So the net comparison is close to zero, and mathematics in particular is the subject where it matters least. A session is shared written working rather than discussion, which transfers to a screen cleanly and needs no room. The energy spent comparing neighbourhoods is better spent on the entry list, which decides something.

sections.heading: Where the help should come from, compared
paragraphs: Once the diagnosis exists, the source of help follows from it, and this corridor offers several. The school's own subject clinic is free and the teacher who marked the work explains it best, which makes it the right answer for a single question about a specific marked answer. Its limit is minutes per student, so it cannot carry a programme or the volume of marked practice a Year 11 student needs.

A centre class near Ibn Battuta provides structure, pace and peer momentum at a lower unit cost, and for a student broadly on track who lacks rhythm that is money well spent. What it cannot do is diagnose: content is set in advance and delivered to the middle of the room, so a student losing method marks will sit through a syllabus review that never mentions working.

One-to-one is the right purchase for a diagnosed problem, for marked paper work, and for scarce entries like Additional Mathematics that no local centre runs. It is the most expensive per hour and the cheapest per grade moved whenever the problem is specific rather than general. Published Dubai rates put a qualified subject tutor online at AED 150 to 300 an hour, against AED 180 to 500 in-home with travel included.

Many families here end up running two together, which is usually correct: a centre revision course for breadth plus one weekly one-to-one session on the thing that is not moving. That costs less than one-to-one across several subjects and uses each model for what it does well. Those rate figures are market figures read in October 2026 and not an IB Gram price list.
bullets: School clinic: free, immediate, right for a single question
Centre class: structure and pace, cannot diagnose an individual
One-to-one: diagnosis, marked practice and scarce entries

sections.heading: Additional Mathematics against a summer bridge
paragraphs: For a student heading to post-16 mathematics there is a fifth comparison worth making, between taking Additional Mathematics as a qualification and doing bridging work over the summer instead. Cambridge 0606 and Pearson 4PM1 bring calculus, logarithms, series and trigonometric identities a year early, examined in their own right, which means the first post-16 term arrives as revision rather than as new content.

The case for the qualification is strongest exactly where this community sits. Families in the Jebel Ali and Dubai South corridor frequently change schools at 16, because full IB Diploma provision nearby is thinner than further north. Meeting a new school, a new teaching style and calculus in the same term is a heavy load, and Additional Mathematics removes one of those three variables permanently.

The practical obstacle is that it is the hardest subject on this page to staff locally in any model. Centres rarely run it, few freelancers have taught it recently, and the cohort is small. That is precisely where an online match earns its keep, since the constraint becomes a calendar rather than a map and the specialism survives the search.

Where a school does not offer the qualification at all, the content still works as a summer bridging syllabus: four to six sessions on function notation, differentiation from first principles and logarithm rules does most of the useful work without an exam entry attached. That is a smaller commitment, it carries no additional examination risk, and it removes most of the first-term shock.

sections.heading: What a mathematics tutor will not do, and our limits
paragraphs: Mathematics carries less assessed coursework than most subjects, which removes one temptation but not all of them. The boundary we state at the first session is simple: a tutor teaches method, questions a student's reasoning, demonstrates technique, marks the student's own work against the board's conventions and writes down the feedback. A tutor does not complete set work, supply answers for submission, or support a student during an assessed task.

On materials, we do not reproduce or distribute Cambridge or Pearson syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables. Those are cited and linked, and sessions work from what the school has issued to the student. A tutor handing over a folder of downloaded board material is distributing something that is not theirs to give, and for unreleased material it is a malpractice exposure for the student.

We also do not guarantee grades. No provider honestly can, and a promised grade is a sales device rather than a teaching plan. What this page has done instead is name where the marks go and how they are typically lost, which is the information a family can actually act on. A page promising a grade 9 without mentioning method marks is selling confidence rather than mathematics.

Finally, we do not describe tutors as examiners without evidence of current status, and examiner status would confer no access to marking, boundaries or paper content in any case. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time between 15:30 and 21:30. No tutor attends a UAE address; home visiting is a service we offer only in India, and there is no IB Gram office in the UAE.
