sections.heading: An honest audit of a Year 11 evening in this community
paragraphs: Before allocating anything, count what exists. A school day, plus a journey of twenty-five to forty-five minutes each way out of a community with no school in it, plus the time to get through the door, change and eat, leaves most Emaar South Year 11 students four to four and a half usable hours on a weekday. Into that go homework from eight to ten subjects, revision, any co-curricular commitment and a tutoring session.

The comparison that makes this concrete is a family living in Green Community, minutes from the school cluster. Same nine subjects, same mocks, same June series, and roughly an hour and a half more usable evening every week. Across a two-year course that is a substantial structural difference and nobody mentions it, which means Emaar South families often conclude their child is working less hard than a classmate when they are working with less time.

The implication is not that these students need more tutoring. It is that the hours have to be allocated rather than spread. Nine subjects dividing four hours evenly produces twenty-six minutes each, which is enough for nothing. The alternative is deliberate inequality: a large share to the subjects where targeted work moves a grade, a small share to the ones where it does not, and acceptance that some subjects get maintenance rather than improvement in a given term.

Mathematics usually has a strong claim on the large share, because its faults are specific and its gains show quickly on past papers. But that claim is to a share of the evening, not to all of it, and it has to be spent on topics that repay it. The next section sorts the subject on exactly that basis.

sections.heading: Which maths topics earn the scarce hours
paragraphs: Not every topic repays the same work, and in a crowded timetable that difference decides what gets funded. The useful measure is examined mark value against time to repair. Reverse percentage appears reliably on both boards, is practised far below its mark value, and takes roughly two sessions to make solid. Reading another chapter of the textbook takes the same two sessions and moves nothing measurable.

Algebraic manipulation is the exception that outranks everything on a different basis. It is not a topic so much as the substrate under simultaneous equations, functions and quadratics, so repairing it treats three apparent weaknesses at once. A student who hesitates over index laws will appear weak in all three, and funding those three separately is how a term disappears. Fix the substrate first and the rest gets cheaper.

After that the high-yield list is short and specific. The area and volume scale factors for similar shapes: short, examined often, forgotten reliably. Full transformation descriptions, where omitting the centre or scale factor costs the mark. Tree diagrams drawn fully before calculating. Bearings sketched with labelled north lines. The supplied formula list, read once at home. Each of these is two sessions or less and each appears in papers every series.

What should be last in the queue, not never but last, is broad content coverage of topics the student can already attempt. It is the default purchase in this market because it feels thorough and because nobody has to decide anything. In a week with four usable evening hours and nine subjects it is the least defensible use of a maths slot, and the table makes the comparison explicit so a family can choose rather than drift.

sections.heading: The formula list: twenty minutes, real marks
paragraphs: Both Cambridge and Pearson supply a formula list in the examination, and most candidates meet theirs for the first time in the hall. That produces two specific losses. The first is time spent deriving or recalling something printed two pages into the booklet in front of them. The second, less obvious, is a candidate assuming something is supplied when it is not, and arriving at a question with no way into it.

The fix costs twenty minutes at home, weeks in advance. Read the list, annotate which formulas are provided, and make a short separate list of what has to be known. That second list is usually far shorter than students fear, which is itself worth discovering: a student who believes they must memorise everything revises inefficiently and anxiously, and a student who knows the eight things not on the sheet revises those.

In a nine-subject week this matters out of proportion to its size, because it is one of very few actions that costs almost nothing and returns reliably. It is also work a student can do alone, which is the right kind of task to hand off when tutor hours are scarce. A tutor's role here is to say it once, set it, and check it happened, rather than to spend a session reading the booklet aloud.

The adjacent habit is knowing where things are rather than what they say. Under time pressure, flicking to the right page quickly is a different skill from knowing the formula exists, and it is practised by using the list during timed homework rather than only in the examination. Students who have had the sheet beside them for every past paper since January do not lose time to it in June.

sections.heading: Producing tier evidence inside a busy year
paragraphs: A Core entry in Cambridge or a Foundation entry in Pearson caps the grade available, however hard the revision. That makes the entry decision the highest-leverage event in the two years, and it usually happens quietly in Year 10 on the basis of a term's class performance. Reopening it is possible and requires a specific document: a full higher-tier paper, sat under timed conditions, marked against the official scheme.

Producing that document is harder in a crowded week than it sounds, which is why most families who intend to never do it. A full Extended Paper 4 takes over two hours, and in an Emaar South weekday evening of four usable hours that is not available alongside homework. It has to go on a weekend morning, deliberately scheduled, with the marking done inside forty-eight hours while the student still remembers their reasoning.

The timing also matters. Entry deadlines are handled by the school as examination centre and fall months before the papers, so evidence produced in the spring of Year 11 arrives after the decision is fixed. A term of Year 10 work building towards a timed higher-tier paper, taken to the subject lead before the entry closes, is the version that works. A family doing this in Year 10 gets a different product for the same money than one doing it later.

If the ceiling is discovered late, one option remains. The November series exists with a fresh entry, which means a candidate who hits a Core ceiling in June can be entered at Extended for November with an autumn term of properly aimed preparation behind them. That decision has to be made in the days after August results rather than in October, because the entry goes through the school months before the papers.

sections.heading: From the mock to June, with nine subjects competing
paragraphs: The mock is the fixed point a revision block should be built around, not the examination, because it is the next piece of real evidence anyone will have. Mock windows differ by several weeks between the clusters Emaar South families travel to, so the first question is when your own school's is rather than when a neighbour's was.

After the mock, the plan narrows. An eight-week block of two sessions a week is sixteen sessions, and in a nine-subject week those sixteen have to be aimed by the script rather than by the syllabus. Week one reads the mock and teaches nothing: whether the paper was finished, whether losses are concentrated or spread, whether marks went on content the student lacks or on checking habits they skipped. Those three findings produce three different plans from one grade.

The specifically crowded-timetable adjustment is that maths cannot have all sixteen sessions if two other subjects also came back weak. In that case the honest answer is to run a shared technique block first, because command-word reading, graph technique, significant figures and answer-length matching appear across maths and all three sciences at once. Four sessions treating those pays into four subjects, which is better arithmetic than four sessions of maths content.

The final fortnight is pacing, and in this community it should be short and frequent rather than long and occasional. Three or four sixty-minute sessions a week, timed sections only, with question order and time allocation practised explicitly. Nothing new. A ninety-minute session in the final week of a nine-subject year tends to end with twenty minutes of nothing useful happening, which is time the student does not have.

sections.heading: Additional Mathematics as an extra claim on the evening
paragraphs: Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606 is offered by some schools in the arc Emaar South families use and not by others a few kilometres away. Where it is offered it is a genuine advantage for a student heading to A Level mathematics or IB Analysis and Approaches, because it covers calculus, further trigonometry, vectors and logarithms a year before their peers meet them.

What families underestimate is that it is a separate subject in practice as well as on paper. The overlap with 0580 is smaller than students expect, particularly in calculus, which means it needs its own revision slot. In a Year 11 week already holding eight or nine subjects and a school run, that is a real additional claim on hours rather than a free extension of the maths one.

The implication is that it should be budgeted in time as well as money. A student taking 0606 alongside 0580 who has one maths slot a week is effectively giving each syllabus half a slot, which serves neither. The workable arrangements are either two separate slots with the same tutor, or a decision to let 0606 run on the student's own work with occasional review while the paid hours go to the main entry.

Which of those is right depends on the destination. If the student is heading to A Level Further Mathematics or IB Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, the 0606 content is an investment and deserves real time. If the grade matters less than the main maths grade, the honest advice is to let it have the cheaper arrangement and protect the hours for 0580. That is a conversation worth having explicitly rather than letting the timetable decide by default.

sections.heading: What a local maths tutor costs from this address
paragraphs: The published Dubai bands separate by whether anybody drives. Qualified subject tutors online sit at AED 150-300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150. In-home one-to-one is AED 180-350 on Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table, with independent home tutors quoted up to AED 500 once travel is priced into the hour. At the budget end Tutopiya advertises from AED 33-52 and EdFlik from AED 45-65.

From Emaar South the in-home figure sits at the top of its band, because the tutor absorbs the same twenty-five to forty-five minute journey the student just made. The monthly packages published in this market make it plainest: AED 799 a month for eight online sessions against AED 1,599-1,799 a month for four in-home sessions of two hours. Bestimate's monthly estimates for one hour a week run AED 240-600 budget, AED 600-1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist examination-year support.

There is a scheduling cost beneath the money that matters more in a crowded week. A tutor who has committed ninety minutes of travel to your address fits one session that evening, which means you take the slot their route allows rather than the slot your child can actually work in. In a week with four usable evening hours, being assigned the wrong hour is not an inconvenience; it is the difference between a session that produces something and one that does not.

Every figure above belongs to the provider named and is published by them. None is an IB Gram price: our conversation starts with a free trial lesson and a written priority list. Three of the six most visible providers competing for these searches publish no price at all and two quote in US dollars, which no Emaar South household transacts in, so a checkable number is itself unusual here.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the breaks and the last fortnight
paragraphs: In a nine-subject year the calendar does most of the allocating, and three periods behave differently from ordinary term weeks. During Ramadan the school day shortens, which also shortens the journey, so an Emaar South student is home earlier even though less of the afternoon is useful. Sessions move after iftar and shorten to sixty minutes, and the content shifts to procedural work: ratio drill, transformation descriptions, formula-list use, graph reading.

The protected daily practice is worth reducing rather than dropping. Ten minutes maintained through Ramadan costs far less than restarting a habit in April, and in a crowded year habits are the only thing that survives. The same applies to self-marking: it takes two minutes, it keeps the diagnosis alive, and abandoning it means the next session starts from scratch.

The breaks are where the work that needs uninterrupted hours belongs, and in this community they return more than they do to a family living beside a school, because both the workload and the journey vanish. A full timed Paper 4 marked and reviewed inside forty-eight hours is break work. So is the timed higher-tier paper that reopens a tier decision. So is catching up a topic that was never covered properly.

The final fortnight is the one period where frequency beats length. Three or four sixty-minute sessions a week, timed sections only, question order and time allocation practised explicitly, and a one-page list for the night before each paper. Nothing new. In a week where nine subjects are all demanding attention, concentration rather than available time is what runs out, and short sessions respect that in a way a ninety-minute block does not.

Produced before the entry deadline it can move a ceiling; produced afterwards it can only confirm one.

whyPoints.title: Working saved week to week
whyPoints.description: Sessions are written on a shared digital surface that persists, so the same algebraic slip in October and February is visible rather than re-diagnosed from memory. In a year where nothing has spare time, not repeating a diagnosis is worth a session on its own.

whyPoints.title: No regulator claims and no UAE centre
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, Cambridge or Pearson approval, accreditation or partnership and operates no office or centre in the UAE. The MoHRE private tuition work permit, free for two years, is the real credential for an individual tutor and one worth asking to see.

faqs.question: How much evening does a Year 11 student in Emaar South actually have?
faqs.answer: Four to four and a half usable hours on a weekday. A school day, plus twenty-five to forty-five minutes of travel each way out of a community with no school in it, plus arrival, changing and eating, consumes the rest. Into those hours go homework from eight to ten subjects, revision, any co-curricular commitment and a tutoring session. A family in Green Community, minutes from the school cluster, has roughly ninety minutes more every week against an identical workload.

faqs.question: Which maths topics are worth funding in a crowded week?
faqs.answer: Algebraic manipulation first, because it is the substrate under simultaneous equations, functions and quadratics, so repairing it treats three apparent weaknesses at once. Then ratio and reverse percentage, which appear every series on both boards and take about two sessions. Then the area and volume scale factors for similar shapes, full transformation descriptions, and tree and Venn diagrams drawn properly before calculating. Each is two sessions or less. Broad content revision comes last, however thorough it feels.

faqs.question: Why does reverse percentage come up so often as a priority?
faqs.answer: Because it has the best ratio of examined mark value to repair time in the subject. It appears reliably on both Cambridge and Pearson papers, the method is procedural, and most candidates have an instinct to divide where they should multiply that is simple to unlearn with drill. Two sessions usually makes it solid. In a week where nine subjects are competing for four hours, a topic that is reliably examined and fixable in two sessions is exactly where a maths slot should go first.

faqs.question: Is it worth spending a session on the formula list?
faqs.answer: Not a session; twenty minutes of the student's own time at home, weeks in advance. Both Cambridge and Pearson supply a formula list, and most candidates meet theirs in the examination hall, where they lose time deriving something printed two pages in, or assume something is supplied when it is not. Reading and annotating the list, and making a short separate list of what must be known, is the cheapest action available. The tutor's job is to set it and check it happened.

faqs.question: When can an Emaar South student sit a full timed paper?
faqs.answer: On a weekend morning, scheduled deliberately. A full Extended Paper 4 takes over two hours and does not fit a weekday evening that already holds homework from nine subjects after a long journey. The marking should follow within forty-eight hours, while the student still remembers what they were thinking on each question, because that memory is most of the diagnostic value and it decays faster than families expect. School breaks work equally well and remove the journey entirely.

faqs.question: Can a tier decision still be changed in Year 11?
faqs.answer: Rarely, and that is the point of raising it in Year 10. Entry is handled by the school as examination centre with a deadline months before the papers, so evidence produced in the spring of Year 11 arrives after the decision is fixed. What does work is a term of targeted Year 10 work ending in a full timed higher-tier paper marked against the official scheme, taken to the subject lead before entries close. If the ceiling is found late, a November entry at the higher tier is the remaining route.

faqs.question: Does Additional Mathematics fit into an already full timetable?
faqs.answer: Only with its own slot, which is the part families underestimate. Cambridge 0606 covers calculus, further trigonometry, vectors and logarithms beyond 0580, and the overlap is smaller than students expect, so one maths hour split between the two syllabuses serves neither. The workable options are two separate slots with the same tutor, or a deliberate decision to let 0606 run on the student's own work with occasional review while paid hours protect the main entry.

faqs.question: Should maths get more hours than the sciences?
faqs.answer: Usually a larger share, but not at the cost of a shared technique block. Command-word reading, graph technique, significant figures and answer-length matching appear in maths and all three sciences at the same time, so four sessions treating them pays into four subjects. That is better arithmetic than four sessions of maths content when several subjects came back weak. After that block, maths generally earns the biggest single share because its faults are the most specific and the gains show fastest.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram teach IGCSE maths at Emaar South homes?
faqs.answer: No. Home visits are a service IB Gram runs in India only and no tutor is sent to any UAE address. Students here are taught live one-to-one over video on Gulf Standard Time, with working written on a shared digital surface that is saved week to week. In a crowded year that record is worth real time, because the same algebraic slip appearing in October and again in February is visible rather than diagnosed again from memory.

faqs.question: What does the in-home premium cost from this community?
faqs.answer: Published figures put in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 an hour on Bestimate's 2026 Dubai table, with independent home tutors up to AED 500 once travel is priced in, against AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor online. From Emaar South the quote sits at the top of the band because the journey is long. The monthly packages are starker: AED 799 for eight online sessions against AED 1,599-1,799 for four in-home ones. These are market figures, not IB Gram prices.

faqs.question: Is a second weekly maths session worth it before June?
faqs.answer: Usually not until the final run-in. A second session in a week with four usable evening hours displaces the fifteen to twenty minutes of daily practice that built the fluency, so the student receives more teaching and does less mathematics. The exception is the last four to six weeks, where timed whole papers rather than practice are the binding constraint. At that point three or four short sessions a week outperform one or two long ones, because concentration runs out before time does.

faqs.question: Which exam series will my child sit, and does the zone matter?
faqs.answer: UAE candidates sit the June series, with November available as a resit route. Cambridge's February and March series is offered to India only, so planning a block towards it wastes a term. The zone does matter: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative timetable zones, each with its own version, and states that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone timetable. Confirm the zone and the final timetable with the school.

faqs.question: What should the daily fifteen minutes actually contain?
faqs.answer: Whatever the last session named, in small attentive doses. Early in a plan that is usually algebraic manipulation: index laws, rearrangement, algebraic fractions. Later it becomes recognition practice across mixed topics, so the student has to decide what kind of question they are looking at before doing it, which is the skill a paper tests. It should always be self-marked against the scheme before sending, because that is where most of the learning sits and it takes two minutes.

faqs.question: How do the school breaks help a nine-subject student here?
faqs.answer: They remove the school workload and the daily journey at the same time, which in this community returns more than it does to a family living beside a school cluster. That is where the work needing uninterrupted hours belongs: a full timed Paper 4 marked inside forty-eight hours, the timed higher-tier paper that reopens a tier decision, and any topic that was never covered properly. Booking those sessions before the term starts is the best-value scheduling decision available from Emaar South.

faqs.question: What changes during Ramadan for a Year 11 maths plan?
faqs.answer: The school day shortens, which also shortens the journey, so the student is home earlier even though less of the afternoon is useful. Sessions move after iftar and shorten to sixty minutes, with the content shifting to procedural work: ratio drill, transformation descriptions, formula-list use and graph reading. The daily practice is worth cutting to ten minutes rather than dropping, because restarting a habit in April costs more in a crowded year than maintaining a reduced one through March.

faqs.question: Which schools in this catchment offer the extension maths syllabus?
faqs.answer: It differs between schools a few kilometres apart, and the British-curriculum arc around Al Furjan and Jebel Ali supplies most Additional Mathematics candidates in this corner of Dubai. The reliable answer comes from your own school rather than from any directory, and it is worth asking in Year 9 rather than discovering in Year 10 that the option was never available. If it is not offered, a summer block before A Level or Diploma mathematics closes the same gap.

intro.heading: Work out the date first, then decide what tutoring can realistically do
paragraphs: Most parents arrive at IGCSE mathematics tutoring with a grade in mind and no date in mind. The date is the more useful of the two. A student eleven weeks from a terminal paper and a student eleven months from one need entirely different work, and the mistake families in Emirates Hills make most often is buying the eleven-month programme with eleven weeks left, or the eleven-week crash course when there was time to fix the foundations properly.

So start with the series. Cambridge International runs IGCSE in a June series and a November series, and in the UAE those are the only two your child will sit; the February and March series is offered to India only, so ignore it on a Dubai timetable. Pearson Edexcel runs International GCSE in May or June and again in November. Your child's school has already chosen, entered them, and in most cases decided the tier. Those three facts constrain everything. A Cambridge June candidate has final entries closing in the spring and forecast grades submitted before the series opens; a Pearson November candidate sits papers from late October through to 19 November 2026 and then waits until the following January for results, as the November 2025 cohort did when grades reached students on 22 January 2026.

The second thing to establish is the tier, because in mathematics the tier sets a ceiling on the grade before any revision happens. Cambridge 0580 splits into Core and Extended; Edexcel 4MA1 splits into Foundation and Higher. A Core or Foundation candidate cannot reach the top grades however well they perform, and the decision is normally made by the department during Year 10 or early Year 11 on the evidence of internal assessments. If that decision looks wrong to you, the window to discuss it closes long before the exam, and it closes at the entry deadline, not at the paper.

Third, find out which administrative zone your child's centre sits in. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six zones and publishes a separate timetable for each. The guidance for exams officers is unambiguous about this and states that Cambridge cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam because the wrong version of the timetable was used. Parents very rarely check this; it costs nothing to ask the exams officer which zone the school is in and to work from that timetable rather than from a version found online.

Once those three facts are on the table, the planning becomes concrete. Count backwards from the paper to the mock, from the mock to today, and allocate the weeks. The sections below do that arithmetic in public: what each milestone is, who sets it, what a student should have finished by then, and what a tutor should be doing in the weeks between. Everything here is built around the calendar because for an IGCSE mathematics candidate the calendar is the binding constraint, not the syllabus.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-emirates-hill.programmesIntro: Around Emirates Hills a child reaches IGCSE mathematics through one of a few routes, and each arrives with a different amount of exam experience. The stage your child is at changes whether this term is about building content, choosing a tier, or rehearsing papers under time.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3 into IGCSE
programmes.description: The three years before the IGCSE course begins, taught against a school scheme rather than an external specification. There is no external examination, so gaps accumulate invisibly. Algebraic fluency, fraction and index work, and confidence with negative numbers are the three things that decide how comfortable Year 10 feels.
programmes.countryNote: In Emirates Living the Key Stage 3 years are when tier outcomes are quietly decided. A child who leaves Year 9 shaky on algebraic manipulation tends to be placed in Core or Foundation in Year 10, and that placement sets a grade ceiling two years early. Tutoring at this stage is cheap, unhurried, and the single highest-leverage intervention available.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics
programmes.description: A two-year course examined in the Core tier or the Extended tier. Core candidates sit a non-calculator paper and a calculator paper of ninety minutes each; Extended candidates sit a non-calculator paper and a calculator paper of two hours each. There is no coursework component, so the whole grade rests on terminal papers.
programmes.countryNote: The Cambridge calendar is what shapes the year for most British-curriculum schools near Emirates Hills. Entries close months before the papers, forecast grades are submitted weeks before them, and results reach the centre before certificates follow. Ask the exams officer for the zone timetable and the internal mock dates in the same email; both drive the revision plan.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A
programmes.description: Examined in two papers of two hours each, both with a calculator permitted, tiered as Foundation or Higher. Foundation covers the lower grade range and Higher the upper, with an overlap band. The absence of a non-calculator paper changes revision priorities noticeably compared with Cambridge.
programmes.countryNote: Families sometimes discover mid-year that their child is on Edexcel rather than Cambridge, or the reverse, because the two are discussed interchangeably in conversation. They are not interchangeable: tier names differ, paper counts differ, and calculator rules differ. Read the specification code on the exam entry confirmation and tell your tutor that code, not the word IGCSE.

programmes.name: After IGCSE: A Level or IB Diploma mathematics
programmes.description: The destination that gives IGCSE mathematics its weight. A Level Mathematics and IB Analysis and Approaches Higher Level both assume secure algebra from the Extended or Higher tier. Students who scraped a pass at the top of a lower tier routinely struggle in the first term of either.
programmes.countryNote: This is the argument for taking IGCSE mathematics seriously in a household where the child is heading for engineering, medicine or economics. Schools near Emirates Hills split after sixteen between A Level and the IB Diploma, and both routes assume the Extended or Higher content as a starting point rather than as an achievement.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-emirates-hill.subjectsIntro: IGCSE mathematics is a single qualification assessed through two terminal papers, but the work splits into distinct blocks that reward different revision. The list below names the blocks and what each one costs a candidate who leaves it alone until April.

subjects.name: Number and the non-calculator paper
subjects.description: Fractions, ratio, percentages, standard form, surds at Extended, bounds and accuracy. Cambridge candidates face this without a calculator, which turns a routine topic into a technique topic. Marks go on upper and lower bounds, on percentage change in reverse, and on rounding too early in a multi-step calculation.

subjects.name: Algebra and graphs
subjects.description: Expanding, factorising, rearranging, simultaneous and quadratic equations, inequalities, sequences, and function notation at Extended. This is the block that decides the tier and the block where a weak Key Stage 3 shows up. Factorising a quadratic with a leading coefficient above one separates grades reliably.

subjects.name: Coordinate geometry and transformations
subjects.description: Gradients, intercepts, parallel and perpendicular lines, and the four transformations with their full descriptions. Students lose marks by describing a transformation incompletely: a rotation needs angle, direction and centre, and two of the three earns nothing if the third is missing.

subjects.name: Mensuration and geometry
subjects.description: Area, surface area, volume, arcs and sectors, similar shapes and the circle theorems at Extended. Circle theorems are learnt as diagrams and tested as reasoning chains; candidates who cannot name the theorem they used lose the justification marks even with the right angle.

subjects.name: Trigonometry
subjects.description: Right-angled trigonometry and Pythagoras at both tiers, with the sine and cosine rules, area of a triangle and three-dimensional problems at Extended. The reliable failure is a non-right-angled triangle attacked with basic ratios, and bearings questions where the diagram is never drawn.

subjects.name: Probability and statistics
subjects.description: Averages from tables, cumulative frequency, histograms with unequal intervals, tree diagrams and conditional probability at Extended. Histograms with unequal class widths cost more marks per question than any other statistics topic because frequency density is taught once and tested in context.

subjects.name: Vectors and matrices
subjects.description: Column vector arithmetic, magnitude, position vectors and geometric proofs using vectors. The proofs are the sticking point: students compute correctly and then do not write the sentence that makes the result a proof, which is where the final marks sit.

subjects.name: Calculus at Extended level
subjects.description: Differentiation of simple polynomials, gradients of curves, and stationary points where the specification includes them. Light in volume and heavy in marks, and frequently the last topic taught, which means it is the topic most often met for the first time in a mock paper.

subjects.name: Exam technique and command words
subjects.description: Show that, work out, calculate, give an exact answer, write down. Each licenses different work and each has a marking consequence. A candidate who writes an answer with no working on a show-that question has scored nothing, and this single habit costs more marks across a paper than any content gap.

sections.heading: What an IGCSE maths tutor in Emirates Hills can do depends on the weeks left
paragraphs: An IGCSE maths tutor in Emirates Hills is most useful when the work is planned backwards from a known date. Establish three facts before the first lesson: which series your child is entered for, which tier, and which administrative zone the centre sits in. Those three answers determine whether the next period of work is about building content, repairing a tier decision, or rehearsing papers under the clock.

With a year or more in hand the work is content and fluency, and it is unhurried. Algebraic manipulation gets rebuilt properly, the non-calculator habits get established before they are urgent, and tier placement stays a live conversation with the department rather than a fact the family receives. This is also the only window in which a Core or Foundation placement can realistically be revisited, because once the entry is submitted the tier is fixed.

With a term in hand the work is the mock script. A marked mock is a better curriculum than any revision guide because it is specific to this student. Every lost mark gets a topic label and an error type, the clusters get taught, and the same questions get reattempted cold two weeks later. Eight to ten sessions handled this way typically shifts more than twenty sessions of general revision, because nothing is spent on material the student already holds.

With six weeks left the work changes character again and becomes rehearsal. No new content, timed sections rather than whole papers so that review happens while the attempt is fresh, the two papers practised separately because a calculator paper and a non-calculator paper reward different instincts, and attention moved to pacing and the discipline of writing working down. Parents often resist this because it feels like less teaching. It is where the last grade boundary is crossed.

sections.heading: The exam series counted backwards, with the dates the boards publish
paragraphs: Nobody in this market publishes an exam calendar, which is odd, because the calendar is the first thing a parent needs. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Pearson Edexcel runs International GCSE in May or June and again in November, and publishes provisional timetables for future series ahead of time.

The useful thing about those series is not the exam week. It is how far ahead of the exam week everything else sits. Take Pearson's November 2026 International GCSE series as the worked example, because its published timetable makes the point plainly: the papers run from late October to 19 November 2026, but the entry that fixed the tier was filed months earlier in the year, the school's internal mocks sat earlier still, and the grade does not reach the student until January, the November 2025 series having landed on 22 January 2026. The Cambridge June series stretches the same gap wider: entries close in the spring, the papers run in June and results follow in August. A family that starts thinking about tier once revision has already begun is past the only decision that mattered.

The Pearson pattern has the same shape with different numbers. The November 2026 International GCSE final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. That January gap is the one families forget: a November candidate waits roughly two months, which matters if a sixth-form application depends on the grade.

Because provisional timetables can be revised, work from the live official timetable rather than from a date restated on a tutoring page, including this one. Ask the exams officer for the current zone timetable in writing and keep it. The table below sets the milestones out in the order they happen, with the authority that sets each one.

sections.heading: Administrative zones: the timetable error that cannot be undone
paragraphs: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, and publishes a separate version of each timetable per zone. The exams officer guidance states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the centre's zone, and that Cambridge cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam because the wrong version was used. That sentence should be read twice by any parent building a revision plan from a timetable found through a search engine.

The practical consequence is small to fix and large to get wrong. A paper that sits on a Tuesday morning in one zone may sit on a Wednesday afternoon in another. A student who has rehearsed a two-paper sequence in the wrong order has rehearsed the wrong thing, and a family who has booked travel around the wrong dates has a genuine problem that no amount of tutoring resolves.

So the first email of the examination year goes to the exams officer, not the mathematics department, and it asks three questions: which administrative zone is the centre in, which series are my child's mathematics papers in, and what are the internal mock dates. Those answers are administrative facts the office holds and will give you. Everything a tutor plans sits on top of them.

There is a second zone-related point about retakes. If a student misses a paper or performs far below the forecast, the next available series may be months away and in a different part of the academic year, which changes whether a retake fits around a sixth-form start. Ask the exams officer what the next available series for that specification is at that centre before you decide anything about a resit.

sections.heading: Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher: when the ceiling gets set
paragraphs: In IGCSE mathematics the tier decision sets a ceiling on the grade before revision begins, which makes it the most consequential academic decision of Year 10. Cambridge 0580 offers a Core tier and an Extended tier. Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 offers Foundation and Higher. In both cases the lower tier covers the lower part of the grade range and the upper tier the upper part, with an overlap band in the middle.

Departments make the decision on internal evidence, usually across Year 10 and the first term of Year 11, and they make it conservatively because entering a student for a tier they cannot access produces a worse outcome than entering them for a tier they can. That logic is sound in aggregate and occasionally wrong for an individual, particularly for a student who arrived mid-course from a different curriculum and whose early internal assessments measured unfamiliarity rather than ability.

If you think the placement is wrong, the conversation has to happen before the final entry deadline, and for a Cambridge June candidate that falls in the spring, roughly four months ahead of the first paper; the exams officer will give you the exact date from the statement of entry. Bring evidence rather than an opinion: a timed upper-tier paper attempted under supervision, with the script, is worth more than any number of conversations about potential. A tutor can supervise exactly that and hand you the marked script to take to the department.

One honest caveat. Moving a student to the higher tier is right when the content gap is closable in the time left and wrong when it is not, and a tutor who always recommends the move is not giving you advice. The table below sets out what each tier actually involves so the conversation can be about papers rather than about ambition.

sections.heading: The eight weeks after a mock, week by week
paragraphs: A January mock script is the most valuable document an IGCSE mathematics candidate will produce, and in most households it is looked at once and filed. The eight weeks after it arrive with a structure already built into them if the script is used properly, and the structure is the same whether the target is a grade 5 or a grade 8.

The first week is analysis, not teaching. Every lost mark gets two labels: a topic and an error type, where the types are content, method, arithmetic, reading and time. The totals tell you what the next six weeks are for. A script with twenty marks lost to arithmetic and six to content needs a different programme from the reverse, and the grade alone cannot distinguish them.

Weeks two to five are teaching the two or three largest content clusters, with the deliberate decision to ignore the smaller ones. Trying to fix everything in six weeks fixes nothing. Weeks six and seven are reattempts, cold, of the same questions that were lost, which is the only evidence that the teaching held. Week eight is timed rehearsal on fresh material, both papers separately.

The table sets this out as a plan you can run with or without a tutor. The one thing that does not work is reading through a revision guide front to back, because it spends most of its time on material the student has already demonstrated they hold.

sections.heading: What a marked script tells you that the grade never will
paragraphs: A mock grade is a summary statistic and it hides the thing you need. Two students can both score a grade 6 for entirely different reasons: one has secure method across the paper and loses marks to arithmetic slips, the other has strong arithmetic and cannot start the harder algebra. Those two students need opposite programmes, and the grade cannot tell them apart.

Reading the script is the fix, and it takes about forty minutes. Work through it question by question and record, for every mark not awarded, which topic the question sat in and why the mark went. Content means the student did not know the method. Method means they knew it and applied it incompletely. Arithmetic means the method was right and the number was wrong. Reading means they answered a question that was not asked. Time means the attempt was not made.

The distribution is the diagnosis. Heavy content losses concentrated in two topics is the easiest and fastest thing to fix. Heavy method losses spread across many topics usually means the student is not writing working down, which is a habit rather than a knowledge problem and responds within a fortnight. Heavy time losses in the last section of the paper is a pacing problem with its own specific remedy. Heavy arithmetic losses point at checking routines.

This is also how you judge whether tutoring is working, and it is a better test than how the sessions feel. If the error log in March shows the same clusters it showed in January, something is wrong with the approach regardless of how pleasant the lessons are. Ask any tutor to keep the log and to show it to you at the six-week mark.
bullets: Content loss: the method was not known. Fix by teaching, two to three sessions per cluster
Method loss: the method was known and incompletely applied. Fix by working-out discipline
Arithmetic loss: right method, wrong number. Fix by a checking routine, not more content
Reading loss: a different question was answered. Fix by annotating the question before starting
Time loss: the attempt was never made. Fix by triage practice on timed sections

sections.heading: Ramadan, study leave and the shape of the Dubai school year
paragraphs: A revision plan built on a European school calendar does not survive contact with a Dubai one. The academic year here runs from late summer to early summer with a long winter break, a spring break, and a Ramadan period during which school days are shortened and the rhythm of the whole household changes. For an IGCSE candidate sitting papers in the first half of the calendar year, Ramadan frequently lands in the middle of the final preparation window.

The practical adjustments are straightforward once they are planned rather than improvised. Shortened school days free up afternoon hours that are normally unavailable, which is the single biggest scheduling gain of the year for a tutoring plan. Evening energy drops for fasting students, so demanding timed work moves to late morning or early afternoon where the school day allows, and post-Iftar slots suit review and consolidation rather than a first attempt at a hard paper.

Study leave is the other structural opportunity and the one families waste most. Once the school releases candidates, mornings become available, and a mind that has been doing mathematics at six in the evening for two years is markedly sharper at ten in the morning. Timed papers belong in those morning slots. A student who sits every practice paper at nine at night has never rehearsed the conditions they will actually sit in.

Plan the whole stretch on one sheet before it starts: school dates, Ramadan, study leave, the mock, the entry deadline, the papers. Then allocate the sessions. This is unglamorous work that takes an hour and saves a term, and it is the reason this page is organised around the calendar rather than the syllabus.

sections.heading: Private candidates, retakes and the questions to ask the exams office
paragraphs: Not every IGCSE mathematics candidate sits through a school. Students who have moved mid-year, who are home educated, or who want an additional subject the school does not offer may need to enter as private candidates through a centre that accepts them. That route exists in Dubai, but it changes the logistics substantially and it is not something a tutoring service arranges on your behalf.

The differences worth knowing are administrative. A private candidate has to find a centre that accepts external entries for that specification and series, meet that centre's own deadline rather than the board's, and pay the centre's entry fee. Practical and speaking components, where a specification has them, are often the limiting factor in whether a centre will take an external candidate at all. Mathematics has no practical component, which makes it one of the easier subjects to sit externally, but the entry still has to be made months in advance.

Retakes follow the same logic. Cambridge runs a June series and a November series, and the February-March series is India-only. Pearson runs May or June and November. A student who misses a target in a June series can often re-sit in November and receive results in the following January, which may or may not fit the sixth-form timeline. That decision should be made with the exams officer and the sixth-form admissions contact in the same conversation, before results day rather than after it.

The permit question belongs here too, because it is one of the few things a parent can verify directly. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated: the private tuition work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation free of charge, and is valid for two years. Individuals tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so treat any specific figure you are quoted with suspicion.

sections.heading: Starting this week, with the date in front of you
paragraphs: Getting started is a short process and it begins with three administrative answers rather than with a lesson. Send us the specification code from your child's exam entry, the series and tier, the mock date, and the marked mock script if one exists. Add two evening windows that survive a normal Emirates Hills week. That is enough to match a tutor who knows the right specification and to plan the weeks that are actually available.

Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video with a shared whiteboard. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For a calendar-driven subject that turns out to be an advantage rather than a compromise, because the binding constraint on in-home tutoring in Emirates Living is the tutor's drive, and the drive is what pushes a session past the hour when a tired Year 11 student can still do mathematics.

If no tutor on the right specification is free in your window, we will say so and offer a different slot rather than putting a Cambridge specialist in front of an Edexcel candidate. The specifications tier differently and reward different exam habits, and with eight weeks left that difference is not cosmetic.

The free trial lesson is a full session with no payment and no card details taken. Use it to watch one thing in particular: whether the tutor opens the mock script in the first ten minutes. A tutor who starts from the script is planning backwards from the date. A tutor who starts from chapter one is not.

whyPoints.title: Facts you can check yourself
whyPoints.description: Every exam date on this page is attributed to Cambridge or Pearson and every regulatory fact to a UAE government source. Timetables can be revised, so we tell you to work from the live official version rather than from a tutoring page, including this one.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE maths series should my child be entered for?
faqs.answer: That decision usually sits with the school rather than the family. Cambridge International runs IGCSE in a June series and a November series, and a UAE candidate sits one of those two; the February and March series is available to India only. Pearson Edexcel runs International GCSE in May or June and again in November. The series affects everything downstream: the entry deadline, the mock timing, the forecast-grade date and when results arrive. Ask the exams officer which series your child is entered for and which administrative zone the centre sits in, then plan the revision backwards from the published timetable for that zone rather than from a generic one.

faqs.question: How far ahead of the exam does the entry deadline fall?
faqs.answer: Further than most families expect. Pearson's November 2026 International GCSE papers run from late October to 19 November 2026, and the entry that fixed the tier for them was filed months earlier in the year. The Cambridge June series opens the gap wider again: entries close in the spring, roughly four months ahead of the first paper, and the exact date sits on your centre's statement of entry. Anything that depends on the entry, above all the tier decision, has to be settled before that deadline rather than during the revision period. Check the live key dates for your child's series on cambridgeinternational.org or qualifications.pearson.com, since published dates can be revised.

faqs.question: What is a Cambridge administrative zone and why should I care?
faqs.answer: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones and publishes a separate timetable for each. The exams officer guidance states plainly that it is essential to use the correct version for the centre's zone, and that Cambridge cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong version was used. A paper sitting on a Tuesday morning in one zone may sit on a Wednesday in another. Ask your exams officer which zone the school is in and work from that timetable, not from one found through a search engine.

faqs.question: When does the Core or Extended tier decision become final?
faqs.answer: At the final entry deadline, which is months before the paper. For a Cambridge June candidate that falls in the spring, well before the papers, and for a Pearson November candidate it was settled long before the late-October start. Departments decide on internal evidence across Year 10 and the first term of Year 11, and they decide conservatively, which is sound in aggregate and occasionally wrong for a student who arrived mid-course from another curriculum. If you want the placement revisited, the conversation must happen before the entry closes and it needs evidence: a timed upper-tier paper sat under supervision, with the script, carries more weight than an opinion about potential.

faqs.question: Can my child move from Foundation to Higher tier during Year 11?
faqs.answer: Only before the entry is submitted, and only if the content gap is genuinely closable in the weeks remaining. Higher tier adds harder algebra, reasoning chains and trigonometry that Foundation excludes, so a move made late means learning new material while also rehearsing papers. Sometimes that is the right call, particularly for a student whose early internal assessments measured unfamiliarity rather than ability. Often it is not. A supervised timed Higher paper settles the question better than a discussion, and the marked script is what the department will respond to.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start IGCSE maths tutoring in the spring term?
faqs.answer: No, but it changes what the tutoring should be. With six to eight weeks left the work is rehearsal and targeted repair, not a tour of the specification. Start from the marked mock script, label every lost mark by topic and error type, teach the two largest content clusters and deliberately ignore the smaller ones, then reattempt the originally lost questions cold a fortnight later. Finish with timed sections on fresh papers. Families who instead buy a general revision course at that point spend most of the hours on material the student already holds.

faqs.question: When do November IGCSE results reach students in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Later than June results, and the gap catches families out. Pearson's published pattern shows June 2026 results going to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, a two-month wait after the papers rather than a nine-week one. Cambridge publishes its own release date to Direct for each series, with certificates following some weeks later. If a sixth-form place or a school transfer depends on the grade, confirm the exact release date for your child's series with the exams officer before deciding on a November entry, because a January grade arrives after a good many offers have already moved.

faqs.question: What should the eight weeks after a mock actually contain?
faqs.answer: Week one is analysis with no teaching: every lost mark labelled by topic and by error type, which produces a ranked list of clusters. Weeks two to five teach the two or three largest clusters and deliberately ignore the rest. Weeks six and seven are cold reattempts of the questions originally lost, which is the only proof that the teaching held. Week eight is timed rehearsal on fresh papers with no new content. Reading a revision guide front to back is the common alternative and it spends most of its hours on material already secure.

faqs.question: Do Cambridge 0580 and Edexcel 4MA1 cover the same mathematics?
faqs.answer: They overlap heavily and differ in ways that matter for exam preparation. Cambridge splits into Core and Extended and sets a non-calculator paper alongside a calculator paper. Edexcel splits into Foundation and Higher and permits a calculator in both papers, each two hours long. That single difference changes revision priorities: a Cambridge candidate needs non-calculator technique rehearsed as its own skill, while an Edexcel candidate does not. Check the specification code on the exam entry confirmation rather than assuming, because the two boards are often discussed interchangeably in conversation.

faqs.question: How should a revision plan handle Ramadan?
faqs.answer: By planning for it rather than improvising around it. Shortened school days free up afternoon hours that are normally unavailable, which is the largest single scheduling gain in the Dubai academic year for a tutoring plan. Energy drops in the evening for fasting students, so demanding timed work moves earlier in the day where the school timetable allows, and post-Iftar slots suit review and consolidation rather than a first attempt at a difficult paper. Put Ramadan, school dates, study leave, the mock and the exam window on one sheet before the term starts and allocate sessions against it.

faqs.question: How should we use study leave for maths revision?
faqs.answer: For timed papers in the morning, which is the opportunity most families miss. Once the school releases candidates, mornings become available for the first time in two years, and a student who has done mathematics at six in the evening throughout the course is noticeably sharper at ten in the morning. Exams are sat in the morning, so rehearsing at that hour rehearses the real conditions. Keep afternoons for review of the morning's attempt while it is fresh, and resist the temptation to fill study leave with new content.

faqs.question: Can my child sit IGCSE maths as a private candidate in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Yes, through a centre that accepts external entries for that specification and series, although the logistics change. The centre sets its own deadline ahead of the board's and charges its own entry fee, and subjects with practical or speaking components are often the hardest to place externally. Mathematics has no practical component, which makes it one of the more straightforward subjects to sit as a private candidate, but the entry still has to be made months in advance. Contact centres directly; arranging an entry is not something a tutoring service does for you.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does UAE equivalency require?
faqs.answer: The published British-track requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five. Candidates also need one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One widely ranking tutoring page states six subjects, which does not match the published rule. Verify the current requirement on the Ministry of Education's own channels, since equivalency is a process your family completes with the Ministry rather than something a tutor performs.

faqs.question: What is a forecast grade and does tutoring affect it?
faqs.answer: A forecast grade is the school's prediction of a candidate's outcome, submitted to the board ahead of the exam. For a Cambridge June candidate the school submits it before the series opens, on the schedule Cambridge publishes for that series. It is used administratively by the board and, in practice, often informs sixth-form conversations. Tutoring does not change a forecast directly, but the evidence the department uses to set it is internal assessment and mock performance, so work that lands before the mock has more influence on the forecast than work that lands after it. Ask the school when forecasts are compiled.

faqs.question: Should we book one long session or two shorter ones each week?
faqs.answer: For mathematics with an exam date approaching, two shorter sessions usually beat one long one, because the gap between them is where the practice happens. A ninety-minute block is efficient for teaching new content and inefficient for rehearsal, since concentration on timed work falls away after about forty-five minutes. The pattern that works through a correction block is one session to teach and set work, one later in the week to mark it and reattempt. If the week only has one slot, keep it to an hour and make the between-session task small enough to actually be done.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-green-communi.tutorsIntro: These tutors cover Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE mathematics for Years 9 to 11 across Green Community, Dubai Investments Park, Jebel Ali, Al Furjan and Dubai South, working from the route or tier your child is entered for.

intro.heading: Revision by chapter, examination by question shape
paragraphs: Textbooks are organised by topic and papers are not. A paper asks about bounds of accuracy by giving a measurement to the nearest centimetre and asking for the maximum possible area. It asks about graph transformations by giving a sketch and an equation and asking which transformation maps one to the other. It asks about vectors by giving a diagram and asking for a one-line geometric reason. None of those three are prepared for by rereading the relevant chapter.

That mismatch is the single most common reason a conscientious Year 11 in this catchment revises for a fortnight and scores the same mark. The content was already mostly in place. What was missing was fluency in the shapes the questions take, and the only way to build that is to attempt the shapes and have somebody mark them against the official scheme.

So this page works through the syllabus by question shape rather than by chapter. It maps the topic areas onto the papers they appear in, sets out the ten calculation types that recur across almost every series, names the specific place each topic sheds marks, and describes a past-paper cycle organised by topic rather than by whole paper.

The first thing it needs from you is the code. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 divides candidates into a Core route sitting Papers 1 and 3 and an Extended route sitting Papers 2 and 4, with the Core route capping the attainable grade. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A 4MA1 runs two equally weighted papers across Foundation and Higher tiers. Those are different papers with different emphases, and preparing for the wrong one wastes weeks.

The second thing it needs is the route or tier, and that matters more than most pages admit. A Cambridge Core candidate is not examined on graph transformations, vector proof, the harder trigonometry or Extended-level algebraic fractions at all. Those topics cannot appear on their papers. A tutor teaching them anyway is spending a student's limited weeks on material the examiner will never ask about, while the bounds, ratio, mensuration and percentage work that the Core papers return to repeatedly goes unpractised. Confirming the route is therefore part of the teaching plan rather than paperwork.

Green Community makes a practical difference to one part of this. The community sits inside Dubai Investments Park, low-rise and walkable, with schools close by, and the local market has reasonable depth at IGCSE mathematics because 37% of Dubai's private pupils are on a UK curriculum. Where it thins out immediately is Additional Mathematics 0606 and Pearson's Further Pure 4PM1, for which a radius search here commonly returns nobody at all.

IB Gram teaches live, one-to-one, over video on Gulf Standard Time. We do not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. For mathematics the format suits the work, because the session is a shared surface with the tutor writing a line and the student writing the next.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-green-communi.programmesIntro: Four things a Green Community maths student may be entered for, and each one changes which topics can be examined and how.

programmes.name: Cambridge 0580, Core route
programmes.description: Core candidates sit Papers 1 and 3, covering a reduced topic list with the harder Extended-only material excluded. The route caps the maximum attainable grade, which is its purpose rather than a defect, and it suits a student who could not access the Extended paper meaningfully.
programmes.countryNote: The practical consequence for tutoring is that some topics are genuinely off the table. A Core candidate does not need graph transformations or vector proof, and time spent on them is time taken from the bounds, ratio and mensuration work that the Core papers actually ask about repeatedly.

programmes.name: Cambridge 0580, Extended route
programmes.description: Extended candidates sit Papers 2 and 4, a shorter paper and a longer one, with the full topic list including algebraic fractions, functions and transformations, vectors, more demanding trigonometry and the harder probability work. Full grade range available.
programmes.countryNote: Most students in this catchment heading for A Level or IB Diploma mathematics are on this route, and the two-paper split matters: Paper 2 rewards speed and accuracy on shorter items, Paper 4 rewards sustained multi-part work. Practising only one of them produces a lopsided result.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel 4MA1
programmes.description: Mathematics A, examined through two papers of equal weight at Foundation or Higher tier. The tier sets the grade ceiling in the same way Cambridge's routes do. Examined in a May/June window and a November window, with provisional timetables published ahead and then revised.
programmes.countryNote: The checkable recent dates give the rhythm: the November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students the next day, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026.

programmes.name: Additional Mathematics and Further Pure
programmes.description: Cambridge 0606 and Pearson 4PM1 are separate qualifications taken alongside the main course, introducing differentiation, integration, logarithms and trigonometric identities ahead of A Level. Usually taken by students heading for A Level Mathematics, Further Mathematics or IB Higher Level.
programmes.countryNote: These two codes have the thinnest specialist supply of anything in this catchment. A radius search from Green Community, Dubai Investments Park or Dubai South for a 0606 tutor commonly returns nobody usable, which is the clearest case here where the delivery model changes the outcome rather than the price.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-green-communi.subjectsIntro: Below is the syllabus by topic area, with the question shape each one takes and the specific place marks go. These are the patterns our tutors see in marked papers from the schools serving this catchment.

subjects.name: Bounds and limits of accuracy
subjects.description: A measurement given to the nearest unit, then a maximum or minimum area, speed or density wanted. Students use the stated value rather than the bound, or pair a maximum numerator with a maximum denominator when the minimum was needed.

subjects.name: Algebraic fractions
subjects.description: Simplifying, adding and solving with factorisable numerators and denominators. Marks go on cancelling across an addition rather than after combining, which is an error that produces a tidy wrong answer.

subjects.name: Simultaneous equations, one linear one quadratic
subjects.description: Substitution then a quadratic, usually with two valid solution pairs. Candidates solve for one variable and stop, forfeiting the marks for the second pair and for pairing the values correctly.

subjects.name: Functions and graph transformations
subjects.description: Translations, reflections and stretches, composite and inverse functions. Transformations applied in the wrong order is the dominant loss, and it is a rule to be memorised rather than a concept to be grasped.

subjects.name: Vectors and geometric reasoning
subjects.description: Column and position vectors, then a short reason explaining why two vectors are parallel or three points collinear. Students compute the vector correctly and omit the one-line reason that carries the mark.

subjects.name: Trigonometry beyond right angles
subjects.description: Sine and cosine rules, area of a triangle, bearings and three-dimensional problems. The recurring loss is a diagram never drawn, so the calculation is attempted from the text and the wrong angle is used.

subjects.name: Probability without replacement
subjects.description: Tree diagrams with changing denominators, then combined outcomes. Candidates write the fractions correctly, multiply along one branch, and forget to add the other mutually exclusive path.

subjects.name: Cumulative frequency and box plots
subjects.description: Reading medians, quartiles and interquartile range off a curve, then interpreting the spread. Interpretation sentences carry marks, and a correct quartile with no statement of meaning earns less than it should.

subjects.name: Mensuration and compound shapes
subjects.description: Volumes and surface areas of composite solids, often with a unit conversion embedded. Marks go on cubic and square conversion factors applied as if they were linear.

subjects.name: Ratio, proportion and percentage change
subjects.description: Reverse percentages, repeated change and ratio splitting in context. Reverse percentage is the single most reliable source of lost marks at Core and Foundation, and it is a four-session fix.

sections.heading: The syllabus mapped onto the papers that examine it
paragraphs: Knowing which paper a topic appears on changes how it should be practised. On Cambridge 0580 the Extended candidate meets most topics twice: once as a short item on Paper 2 and once embedded inside a longer multi-part question on Paper 4. Those two encounters test different things. The short item tests whether the method is automatic. The long question tests whether the student can hold a thread through several linked steps while the arithmetic gets messier.

Pearson 4MA1 distributes the same content differently, across two papers of equal weight, which removes the short-and-long distinction and replaces it with a more even demand. For a tutor that changes the practice diet: less emphasis on sprinting through short items, more on consistent accuracy across a full paper with no easier half to bank marks in.

The Core and Foundation routes narrow the topic list rather than softening it, and that narrowing is useful information. A Core candidate does not need graph transformations, vector proof or the harder trigonometry, and a tutor who teaches those anyway is spending the student's limited weeks on content the paper cannot ask about. Confirming the route is therefore not administrative tidiness; it determines what belongs in the plan.

Our first request from a Green Community family is the exam entry statement or a photograph of a past paper, because both carry the code and the route. One photograph settles what will be examined, in what form, on which paper, and it prevents the most expensive mistake available in maths tutoring.

sections.heading: Ten calculations that recur in almost every series
paragraphs: Across series, a small set of calculation types appears again and again, and a student who is automatic at all ten has removed most of the avoidable losses on either board. They are worth listing because they cut across topic boundaries, which is exactly why chapter-based revision misses them.

The ten: reverse percentage; repeated percentage change; ratio splitting in context; upper and lower bounds in a compound measure; unit conversion in two and three dimensions; rearranging a formula where the subject appears twice; solving a quadratic by factorising and by formula; the sine and cosine rules with a diagram drawn first; probability along and across tree branches; and reading an estimate from a cumulative frequency curve with an interpretation sentence attached.

None of those is conceptually hard and all of them are time-sensitive in an examination. A student who has to reconstruct the method for reverse percentage loses ninety seconds and often the mark; a student for whom it is automatic loses neither. That is the difference between knowing a topic and being fluent in it, and fluency is built by repetition with marking rather than by understanding something once.

The practical plan is unglamorous. A short set of these ten, mixed rather than grouped, marked by somebody who is not the student, once a week for six weeks. Mixing matters: grouped practice lets the student know which method to reach for before reading the question, which is exactly the help the paper will not give them.

sections.heading: Where each topic actually sheds marks, in detail
paragraphs: Bounds is the clearest example of a topic that fails for a reason nothing in the chapter addresses. A length is given as 12 centimetres to the nearest centimetre and the question asks for the maximum possible area of a rectangle. The student uses 12. Or, worse, correctly identifies the upper bound for both dimensions when the question asked for a minimum density, where the maximum mass and the minimum volume were needed. That is a reasoning error about which bound goes where, and it is drillable in three sessions.

Algebraic fractions fails by cancelling too early. Faced with two fractions to add, the student cancels a factor that appears in one numerator and the other denominator before combining, producing a clean-looking answer that is wrong. The rule - combine first, then factorise, then cancel - is easy to state and needs enforcing, because the premature cancellation feels like efficiency.

Graph transformations fails on order. Two transformations applied in the wrong sequence produce a different image, and the student who knows what each transformation does individually still gets the composite wrong. This is a rule to memorise, not an insight to reach, and treating it as the latter wastes sessions.

Vectors fails on the reason rather than the computation. Students reach the correct column vector and then write nothing, when the mark is for saying that two vectors are multiples of one another and therefore parallel, or that three points are collinear because two vectors between them share a point and a direction. One sentence, consistently omitted. Trigonometry beyond right angles fails on the missing diagram, and probability without replacement fails on adding, not multiplying.
bullets: Bounds: decide which bound each part of the expression needs, before calculating
Algebraic fractions: combine, then factorise, then cancel - never cancel first
Transformations: the order is a rule to memorise, not a concept to derive
Vectors: write the one-line geometric reason, every time
Probability trees: multiply along, then add across the valid paths

sections.heading: A past-paper cycle organised by topic, not by paper
paragraphs: Most students in this catchment have already done past papers, often many, and their mark has not moved. The reason is nearly always that whole papers were sat untimed, self-marked and filed. Whole-paper practice has a place and it is late in the preparation; earlier, it hides the cause behind a total.

A topic-organised cycle gives different information. Pull ten questions on one topic from several series, sit them under timing, and have them marked against the official scheme. The result is not a score but a diagnosis: the method is secure and the arithmetic is not, or the reverse, or the question is being misread, or a particular sub-type within the topic is the only one failing. That is actionable in a way that a paper total never is.

The marking has to be external, and this is the part students cannot do for themselves. Self-marking systematically over-rewards, because the student knows what they intended to write and reads their own shorthand generously. An examiner-literate reader marks what is on the page: no method line, no method mark; a bound used instead of the stated value, no mark; an unexplained value from the calculator, nothing. Seeing that applied three times changes the behaviour.

sections.heading: The route and tier decision, in topic terms
paragraphs: Most pages discuss Core against Extended, or Foundation against Higher, in terms of grade ceilings. That matters, and the topic consequence matters too, because it changes what a student has to learn at all. A Core candidate is not examined on graph transformations, vector proof, the harder trigonometry or algebraic fractions at the Extended level, and that is a materially smaller body of work.

Read that way, the decision becomes concrete rather than emotional. For a student who can access Extended questions but is losing marks to unwritten method, early rounding and abandoned multi-part questions, moving to Core removes topics they could have learned and caps a grade they could have reached. For a student who cannot begin most Extended questions, Core removes content that was never going to produce marks and concentrates the available weeks on bounds, ratio, mensuration and percentage work that the Core papers ask about repeatedly.

The evidence should be two timed papers, one at each route, marked externally against the official scheme. That takes two hours of a student's week and it replaces a judgement about workload with a judgement about marks. A tutor can tell you from those two scripts whether the losses are habits, which move in weeks, or inaccessibility, which does not.

Then read the destination. Both A Level and IB Diploma routes exist within this catchment, and the mathematics entry grades are usually among the highest a sixth form publishes. Some of them cannot be reached from a Core or Foundation entry. The entry deadline for a route change is set by the school and it arrives earlier than families expect, so the question is worth asking in Year 10 rather than in Year 11.

For mathematics specifically, the mid band is where the useful people mostly are, and the premium bands buy something narrower than families expect. What separates the middle of the band from the bottom of it is usually mark-scheme literacy: knowing that the bound question pays for choosing the right bound rather than for the arithmetic, and marking accordingly. What separates the top of the in-home band from the middle of the online one is frequently a journey.

None of these are IB Gram prices and this page carries no rate card, because the fee depends on the course and level and is quoted after the free trial lesson.
