sections.heading: Establish the board, the code and the tier first
paragraphs: Before any hours are bought, three facts should be in writing from the school. The board. The syllabus code. The tier. Together they decide what grade is arithmetically reachable, and they are the facts a neighbour's recommendation cannot supply because the neighbour's child may be on a different qualification altogether.

The tier does the heavy lifting. Tiered IGCSE mathematics caps the grade at the lower tier: a candidate entered for Cambridge 0580 Core cannot be awarded the top grades, and the same applies to Pearson Mathematics A at Foundation. So a family paying for months of hours to lift a Core candidate into the top band is paying for an outcome the entry has excluded. The reverse error exists too - a student entered for Extended who is not yet fluent faces a whole paper pitched above their current level, which content teaching does not recover.

The code matters for a different reason: past-paper practice has to be on the right board. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 have different paper structures and different calculator permissions, and a student revising with the wrong board's papers is practising unfamiliar question styles and timing. That wastes the best preparation tool in the subject, and it happens most often in exactly the situation this page describes - after a school move inside the eastern suburbs.

The decision on tier belongs to the school, which is right because they hold the data, and it is interrogable. The window is Year 10 into early Year 11, not March. Ask what your child's current performance predicts on each tier and what specifically would have to change by the entry deadline. A specialist reading a marked mock can separate marks lost to fixable technique from marks lost to the paper being pitched too high - which is the whole decision and takes one session.

sections.heading: Mirdif against Al Warqa against Al Mizhar: the honest comparison
paragraphs: Families in the eastern suburbs compare neighbourhoods constantly when looking for tutors, so here is the comparison done properly. What differs between Mirdif, Al Warqa, Al Mizhar and Al Khawaneej is housing, school provision and drive times. What differs much less is the supply of tutors who know your child's specific board and tier, because that is a city-wide variable rather than a street-level one.

What genuinely differs, and in a way that matters, is the curriculum mix. Al Warqa and International City carry heavy Indian-curriculum enrolment; Mirdif itself has British, American, Indian and IB provision within the neighbourhood; the creek-side schools in Festival City and Garhoud skew differently again. So a tutor who is well known and well regarded in one of those households may have built that reputation on a syllabus your child is not sitting. That is the eastern-suburb trap, and it is specific to this part of Dubai.

Drive times do affect in-home pricing. Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 with independent home tutors advertising up to AED 500, against AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor online. Those are city-wide ranges and where a household sits inside them tracks distance from the tutor. From Al Khawaneej, the furthest out, an in-home quote is realistically at the top of the band and the pool willing to come at five in the afternoon is correspondingly small.

Which means the useful comparison is not between suburbs at all. It is between hiring by distance and hiring by syllabus. The table sets out what each neighbourhood offers so the decision can be made on evidence rather than on a sense that somewhere nearby must be better served.

sections.heading: Group class, one-to-one or in-home: the eastern-suburb comparison
paragraphs: This is the comparison most Mirdif families actually face, because the neighbourhood has tuition centres as well as private tutors. Each option is reasonable for something, and each is routinely bought for the wrong thing. The honest division depends on whether your child's problem is common content or specific to their board, tier and habits.

A group class at a centre is cheaper per hour and works for common content revision - a topic the whole room has not grasped, taught once. It works badly where the problem is board-specific, because a room containing Cambridge Core, Cambridge Extended and Pearson Higher candidates can only be taught generically. Note too that a centre with premises in Dubai operates under a KHDA Educational Services Permit, a different licence from an individual tutor's MoHRE permit, and it is reasonable to ask for the number.

One-to-one online sits at AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor and is where diagnosed work belongs, because the session can be aimed at one student's tier, board and marked script. In-home one-to-one at AED 180-350, or up to AED 500 independently, delivers the same teaching plus physical presence - which genuinely helps a younger or easily distracted student, and from the eastern suburbs costs the most because the drive is longest.

Published monthly packages make the trade concrete: about AED 799 a month for eight online sessions against AED 1,599-1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. For maths, where the work is annotated calculation both parties need to see, a shared screen does the job fully. Where supervision is the real need, in-home is worth paying for and plenty of Dubai providers deliver it - IB Gram does not, because home visits are a service we run only in India. One piece of household context: KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for 2026-27, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion.

sections.heading: The question styles that catch transferring students
paragraphs: Content gaps are easy to find and easy to fix. Question-style gaps are neither, because they do not show up on a topic checklist - they show up as a student who knows the maths and scores below expectation. Three specific patterns account for most of it, and all three are teachable in a handful of sessions once named.

The first is the multi-part structured question. IGCSE papers build a question across parts, with earlier answers feeding later ones and marks awarded for method. A student from a system that rewards the final answer will present clean solutions and forfeit method marks, and will abandon a part rather than carry a partial result forward. Teaching them to show working and to use their own earlier answer is worth more than any topic revision.

The second is context. Many IGCSE questions wrap the mathematics in a situation - a journey, a bill, a scale drawing - and the first task is extracting the mathematics from the words. Students arriving from more abstractly presented syllabuses can be excellent at the operation and slow at the extraction, which costs time across a whole paper and therefore costs marks at the end of it.

The third is command words. Show that, prove, hence, explain, estimate: each asks for something specific, and answering the wrong one is capped before the mathematics is read. Hence in particular means use the previous result, and a student who starts again from scratch loses the marks even when the answer is right. Rewriting one question properly against a real mark scheme teaches more than attempting ten.

sections.heading: Counting backwards to the June or November series
paragraphs: UAE candidates sit the June series and the November series. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The February/March series is offered to India only and does not apply to a candidate in Dubai - a distinction that matters particularly in the eastern suburbs, where families with connections to Indian schooling may have heard the February window described as normal.

One Cambridge detail affects planning directly. Every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, warning that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Ask your child's exams officer which zone the centre sits in, in writing, before building any plan around a date found online.

For Pearson, International GCSE exams are available in May/June and November each year. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so work from the live official timetable rather than from any restated dates, including these.

Counted backwards the phases are: board, code and tier confirmed; transfer mapping if the student has moved curricula; steady work or a diagnosed block; the mock round read from marked scripts rather than percentages; then timed papers on the correct board. Resit routes exist in both directions, with entry fees set by the board and the examination centre rather than by any tutor, so ask the school or the centre for that figure.

sections.heading: Scheduling from Mirdif, where two children rarely share a clock
paragraphs: Eastern-suburb school runs are unusually varied, and that is a scheduling fact rather than a complaint. A Mirdif household can have one child at a school inside the neighbourhood and another travelling to Festival City, Silicon Oasis or further west, which means two arrival times and two sensible slots. A tutor who drives can serve one of them.

The practical method is to write down the real arrival time for each child on a normal term-time day: timetabled finish, plus the bus loop, plus the walk, plus the twenty minutes a teenager needs to eat and stop being a passenger. Set the slot after that, and then stop renegotiating it. A session scheduled against the timetable instead loses its first twenty minutes every week, which across a thirty-week school year discards roughly ten hours of tuition - at AED 150-300 an hour, the cheapest available improvement to any arrangement.

Past roughly 7.30pm most Year 10 and Year 11 students produce diminishing work, so the usable weekday window in Mirdif is roughly 4.30pm to 7.30pm depending on the run. Where the week genuinely contains no usable hour - a long westward commute plus clubs plus a sibling's schedule - a weekend slot with a rested student does more than a weekday one forced in against the evidence.

Two Dubai-specific points. School days shorten during Ramadan and the afternoon becomes the least productive part of the day, so a post-Iftar slot often works better; an arrangement that can move survives the month, and one that cannot frequently does not restart afterwards. And over the summer, a family travelling can keep the hour running on Gulf Standard Time or shift it to another time zone, which is not an option when somebody has to drive to a villa in Mirdif.

sections.heading: Checking the tutor, which costs nothing
paragraphs: Two free checks before the first paid hour, and they matter more when a tutor has come via a neighbour's recommendation rather than through any process. The permit first: private tutoring in the UAE is regulated, the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, it is granted free of charge for two years, and individuals offering private tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted at you.

The mechanics are worth knowing because they remove every excuse a tutor might offer. The filing is MoHRE's own service, Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, submitted through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system; it lists no fees and states a two-working-day completion time. Its eligible categories read almost like a census of who actually tutors in a suburb like this one: teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. The Mirdif engineer teaching Edexcel maths on Tuesday evenings qualifies, and so does the Year 13 student two streets away. Two working days and no fee means a working tutor without one has chosen not to have one.

The second check is the arrangement itself, which in a curriculum-mixed suburb comes up often. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Treat it as press-reported and verify against current policy, but decline the arrangement where your child's own maths teacher is paid privately.

And the claims to refuse. No individual tutor in Dubai is KHDA-approved, because that status does not exist for individuals - KHDA regulates schools and issues an Educational Services Permit to training institutes with premises in the emirate. Nobody holds Cambridge or Pearson accreditation as a private tutor. And no provider should supply board syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables as downloads; those get referenced and linked to the board's own site. IB Gram holds no regulator or board accreditation and operates no premises in the UAE.

sections.heading: The first fortnight after a mid-course move
paragraphs: This is the highest-value fortnight available to an eastern-suburb family, and almost nobody uses it. A student who changes school and curriculum mid-course has a window in which the gaps are small and findable. Left alone, those gaps compound quietly and surface three months later as a disappointing mock, by which point the same work costs three times as much to do.

Session one is a comparison rather than a lesson: the new syllabus against what the student has actually covered, topic by topic, using the live syllabus document from the board's own site rather than anybody's summary. The output is a written gap list - usually three to six items, not twenty - that the student, the parent and the new school can all see. That document is the deliverable and it is worth more than any amount of general catch-up.

Session two addresses question style, because that is the gap a topic checklist misses. Multi-part structured questions, contextual wrapping, command words, and the method-mark conventions of the new board. For a student arriving from CBSE this is often the entire problem, and it can be substantially fixed in a single well-aimed session followed by marked practice.

Sessions three and four take the first two items from the gap list, with practice set between and marked at the next. Then the plan gets reviewed against the school's first assessment rather than extended by default. Some students need nothing further. Some need a longer block. Some turn out to be in a tier conversation with the new school, and should be told so. The free trial lesson means the comparison session costs nothing, which is the right price for the most useful hour in the sequence.

faqs.question: Why did a maths tutor recommended by a Mirdif neighbour not suit my child?
faqs.answer: Most often because the neighbour's child is on a different qualification. The eastern suburbs mix British, American, Indian and IB provision within a short drive, and Dubai overall had 227 private schools offering 17 curricula in 2024-25 with Indian at 26% of enrolment and US at 14%. A tutor who is genuinely excellent on CBSE mathematics may have never taught Cambridge 0580 or Pearson 4MA1, where the paper structure, method-mark conventions and calculator rules all differ. Ask any recommended tutor which board and code they have taught before anything else.

faqs.question: My child moved into IGCSE from CBSE. What actually needs fixing?
faqs.answer: Usually question style rather than content. Students arriving from CBSE often have stronger algebraic manipulation and arithmetic speed than their new classmates, and are unfamiliar with the IGCSE habit of building a question across multiple parts in a context, where earlier answers feed later ones and marks are awarded for method shown. A clean solution with the right answer can forfeit method marks. That is a presentation and convention gap, fixable in a single well-aimed session plus marked practice, and it reads on a report as a maths problem.

faqs.question: What do students arriving from an American programme typically miss?
faqs.answer: Surds, upper and lower bounds, circle theorems and some of the geometry work are commonly not yet met, while statistics, data handling and modelling have often been covered earlier and more thoroughly than their new peers have managed. The student is not behind - the sequence was different. A comparison of the live IGCSE syllabus against what has actually been covered usually produces three to six missing blocks rather than a year's worth, and five to eight weeks of targeted support closes them.

faqs.question: Does living in Al Warqa or Al Khawaneej change the tutoring options?
faqs.answer: Only the in-home price and the number of tutors willing to drive. Supply of teachers who know a specific board and tier is a city-wide variable rather than a street-level one, so widening the search from Mirdif to the next suburb does not widen the pool. What it does change is distance: Bestimate's 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 with independent home tutors to AED 500, and an address further east sits near the top of that range. Online, the AED 150-300 qualified-tutor band applies identically everywhere.

faqs.question: Is a tuition centre group class in Mirdif worth it for maths?
faqs.answer: For common content revision, sometimes - a topic the whole room has not grasped, taught once, is reasonable value. For diagnosed work it is poor value, because a room containing Cambridge Core, Cambridge Extended and Pearson Higher candidates can only be taught generically, and nobody there can address one student's tier or command-term habits. A centre with premises in Dubai also operates under a KHDA Educational Services Permit, which is a different licence from an individual tutor's MoHRE permit, and asking for the number is entirely reasonable.

faqs.question: How do I find out which tier my child is entered for?
faqs.answer: Ask the school in writing, and ask for the code alongside it. Tiered IGCSE mathematics caps the grade at the lower tier: a Cambridge 0580 Core candidate cannot be awarded the top grades, and the same applies to Pearson Mathematics A at Foundation. That makes the tier the first thing to establish, because it determines whether the grade you are aiming at is arithmetically available before any teaching affects anything. The decision belongs to the school and the window to discuss it is Year 10 into early Year 11, not March.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether we practise Cambridge or Pearson past papers?
faqs.answer: It matters a great deal, and getting it wrong is common after a school move inside the eastern suburbs. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson Mathematics A 4MA1 have different paper structures, different tiering and different calculator design - Pearson permits a calculator throughout, which shifts the skill balance. A student revising with the wrong board's papers is practising unfamiliar question styles and timing, which wastes the single best preparation tool in the subject. Confirm the code with the school and then use only that board's materials.

faqs.question: Which command words cost the most marks in IGCSE maths?
faqs.answer: Hence is the expensive one. It means use the previous result, and a student who starts the question again from scratch loses the marks even when the final answer is correct. Show that and prove require the argument rather than the answer, so a verified numerical check earns little. Estimate asks for sensible rounding before calculating, not after. Each of these is capped before the mathematics is read if the wrong thing is delivered, and rewriting one question properly against a real mark scheme teaches more than attempting ten.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a maths tutor to a villa in Mirdif?
faqs.answer: No. Home visits are a service we run only in India, and nobody is sent to a UAE address. For a Mirdif, Al Warqa or Al Mizhar family, lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with screen sharing so the marked paper, the correct board's past paper and the mark scheme are visible to both sides and the annotated script stays with the student. From the eastern suburbs that also removes the longest drive in the city from the price, which is where most of the in-home premium here comes from.

faqs.question: What should a Mirdif family do in the first fortnight after changing schools?
faqs.answer: A syllabus comparison, before anything else. One session setting the new board's live syllabus against what the student has actually covered, producing a written gap list - usually three to six items - that the student, the parent and the new school can all see. Then one session on question style and method-mark conventions, which a topic checklist never catches. Left alone, those gaps compound quietly and surface three months later as a disappointing mock, at which point the same work costs several times as much.

faqs.question: How many hours does an IGCSE maths problem usually take to fix?
faqs.answer: It depends on the category, and a marked paper shows that in ten minutes. Question-style and convention problems after a curriculum transfer typically run three to five hours. A single diagnosed topic gap runs two to four. An algebraic fluency rebuild runs eight to fifteen, in short frequent sessions rather than long ones. Whole-paper weakness is twenty hours or more, and at that point the tier conversation matters more than the hours. Nobody can promise a specific grade from any of it, and a provider who does is telling you something.

faqs.question: Which series will an eastern-suburb candidate be entered for?
faqs.answer: The June series or the November series. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series, with Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The February/March series is offered to India only and does not apply to a candidate in Dubai - worth stating plainly here, because families with connections to Indian schooling sometimes hear the February window described as standard. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams are available in May/June and November each year, and the live official timetable is the only source to plan from.

faqs.question: Why would my child's exam timetable differ from a friend's at another school?
faqs.answer: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, warning that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Two candidates sitting the same syllabus at different centres can therefore face different dates and times. It is one written question to your child's exams officer, and the answer should be in hand before any revision plan is built around a particular date.

faqs.question: What time should a session start for a Mirdif student with a long school run?
faqs.answer: After the real arrival time on a normal day, not after the timetabled finish. Eastern-suburb runs vary from a short hop to a school inside Mirdif to a long westward drive, and households with two children often have both at once. Work out the finish, plus the bus loop, plus the walk, plus the twenty minutes a teenager needs to eat and decompress. A session losing its first twenty minutes weekly discards roughly ten hours across a thirty-week year, which at AED 150-300 an hour is the cheapest improvement available.

faqs.question: Does a resit cost anything beyond the tutoring?
faqs.answer: Yes - entry fees, which are set by the board and the examination centre rather than by any tutor and differ between centres, so the figure has to come from your child's school or the centre you would enter through. Both boards run two series a year, so a June result can be addressed in November and a November result in the following May or June. Read the mark breakdown before deciding: a candidate who was close and lost marks across the paper to timing and working is in a very different position from one who was a long way off.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-mirdif.closingHeading: Confirm the qualification before you take the recommendation
dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-mirdif.closingBody: If you are looking for an IGCSE maths tutor in Mirdif, the step that saves the most is also the cheapest: get the board, the syllabus code and the tier from the school in writing, because in a suburb this curriculum-mixed a neighbour's recommendation may rest on a different qualification entirely. Then send the last marked paper, and say if your child has moved curricula mid-course. You will get a named tutor who has taught that board, a written gap list if a transfer is involved, and a free trial lesson that functions as the diagnosis. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; home visits are a service we run only in India.

intro.heading: The evening already has maths in it. Plan around that
paragraphs: IGCSE maths is unusual among school subjects in how often it sets work. Most departments give maths homework three to five nights a week, in short pieces, because that is how the subject is taught and it is the right way to teach it. Any tutoring arrangement that ignores this ends up competing with the school's own maths for the same twenty minutes, and the student resolves the conflict by doing whichever one gets checked. That is the school's.

So the first question is not who to hire but how the session will dovetail with work that already exists. A tutor who sets an additional exercise sheet has created a choice the student will make badly. A tutor who asks what the school set this week, marks that, and teaches from the errors in it has made the existing homework more useful without adding an hour to the evening. The second approach costs the same and produces considerably more.

The timing makes it tighter. The schools serving this district finish between roughly 2:45pm and 3:30pm. A student at a school inside the district or in Nad Al Sheba is home within twenty minutes; one travelling from Al Safa, Al Barsha or further west is in afternoon traffic, and the final stretch into a gated community adds to it, so arriving between 3:45pm and 4:15pm is routine. After clubs, fixtures and the twenty minutes a fourteen-year-old needs to arrive properly, the usable window is narrow and already partly spoken for.

A near-me search tightens it further, which is the part worth knowing before you ring round. The tutors who answer it are those prepared to drive here, and a tutor leaving the western cluster at four is in the same traffic your child was, plus the gated access at this end. Arrival between a quarter to five and a quarter past is normal, which pushes the session into the hour the evening can least afford and leaves the school's maths homework to be done at nine.

IB Gram delivers IGCSE maths tuition to Mohammed Bin Rashid City as one-to-one lessons over live video on Gulf Standard Time, so the hour starts when the student is settled rather than when a tutor has cleared the gate. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. The sections below show how to dovetail with school work, why Year 10 and Year 11 are different problems, and how the two-year course looks term by term.

Nothing here promises a grade. It gives you a way to decide how much the week can absorb and how to make the hour you buy improve the work your child is already doing, which in a subject that sets homework most nights is the most useful thing a tutor can do.

A student heading for A Level Mathematics or IB Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level needs algebraic fluency that a borderline IGCSE grade does not evidence, and a short bridging block in that summer does more than weekly support in a crowded Year 12 term.

sections.heading: Dovetailing with the maths homework your child already has
paragraphs: This is the design principle that separates useful IGCSE maths tutoring from expensive duplication. School maths sets short work most nights. A tutor who adds their own exercises has put two sets of maths into the same evening, and a fourteen-year-old resolves that by doing the one that gets collected. The homework that gets collected is the school's, so the tutoring work quietly stops being done and the hour becomes a conversation.

The alternative costs nothing extra and works considerably better. The tutor asks what the school set, marks it before the session, and arrives knowing the error pattern. The hour is then spent on the pattern rather than on the questions: the student is not slow at question seven, they are slow at rearranging, and that distinction is the entire value of a trained marker. The student goes back to the school's own work with a correction to apply, and the next week's homework becomes the next week's evidence.

There is a second benefit that matters more than it sounds. Work set by the school is work the school's teacher sees, so improvement shows up where it counts: in classwork, in predicted grades and in the teacher's judgement about tier entry. Tutoring that runs on a parallel track produces a student who is better at the tutor's exercises and unchanged in the eyes of the department that will enter them for the examination.

The table sets out how the division of labour should look. Read the right-hand column as the test of whether an arrangement is dovetailed or duplicated. If a tutor cannot tell you what the school set last week, they are running a parallel track, and in a subject that sets homework most nights that is the most common way a household's money and a student's evenings are both wasted at once.

sections.heading: Year 10 has room. Year 11 does not
paragraphs: Households in this district usually ask for a maths tutor in Year 11, and Year 10 is when it would have worked. That is not a reproach, because nothing has gone visibly wrong in Year 10, but the scheduling difference between the two years is large enough to change what tutoring can achieve in each.

A Year 10 week has nine subjects setting work, no mock season, no school revision programme running in the evenings and no examination fortnight in sight. There is room for a weekly session and for a nightly practice habit to be established while it is still possible to establish one. Algebraic fluency takes a term or two to build and a Year 10 term is available. The same work compressed into February of Year 11 is not fluency-building; it is triage.

A Year 11 week has the same nine subjects, plus mock examinations, plus the school's own revision provision occupying some evenings, plus coursework or spoken components in other subjects falling due. There is room for one surgical block and essentially nothing else. The right Year 11 purchase is four to six sessions beginning the week after mock results, aimed at named losses from the marked script and finishing before the school's final revision programme intensifies.

The table compares the two years directly. Read it as an argument for acting a year earlier than feels necessary, which is the single cheapest piece of advice on this page. A Year 10 block of eight sessions costs less than a Year 11 block of eight sessions achieves, because the Year 10 version has time to compound and the Year 11 version has to pick its battles.

sections.heading: When a session fits, and the twenty-minute rule
paragraphs: The timing chain is specific and worth working through once: when the school day ends, how long the journey home takes at that hour, the twenty minutes a student needs before they can work, and therefore when a session can begin without being wasted. That third element is the one households skip, and it is the cheapest improvement available.

The twenty-minute rule is simply that a student who has been in school since half past seven cannot start working the moment they walk through the door. They need to put a bag down, eat something and stop being in transit. A session scheduled for the minute of arrival buys an hour of someone present and unavailable. Twenty minutes later the same hour is worth considerably more, and it costs nothing to arrange.

The table applies the chain to the school clusters serving this district, with the in-home comparison in the final column. The in-home figure is consistently about forty-five minutes later, because the tutor meets the same traffic plus gated access at this end. For maths that difference is material rather than cosmetic: the later the session, the more of it becomes conversation and the less becomes timed work, and the school's own homework gets pushed towards nine o'clock.

One further scheduling rule specific to maths. Place the session before the homework rather than after it, where the week allows. A session that ends at half past five leaves a student able to apply the correction to that night's work immediately, which is when it sticks. A session at seven leaves the homework already done, wrongly, and the correction waiting a week to be tested.

sections.heading: Term by term across the two-year course
paragraphs: Scheduling advice is more useful spread across the course than given as a single rule, because what the week can absorb and what the work is for both change. The table maps the two years in terms rather than weeks, which is the unit a household can actually plan in.

The pattern it recommends is front-loaded, which is the opposite of what most families do. The heavy lifting belongs in Year 10, when fluency can be built and the tier can still be reviewed with evidence. Year 11 autumn belongs to the school's scheme of work and one dovetailed session if a weakness persists. Year 11 spring belongs to the mock, the script and a short surgical block, then to the school's own revision programme.

The term nobody uses is the summer between Year 10 and Year 11, and the holiday weeks within the year. Those are the only genuinely empty evenings in the whole course. Three to five sessions across a holiday week, with a rested student and nothing competing, address a foundation gap properly rather than squeezing it between homework. For households who travel, sessions follow the student provided the time zone is agreed.

One caution before planning around any of it. The school's own calendar governs: mock dates, coursework deadlines in other subjects, the start of revision provision and entry deadlines all belong to the school, and they vary and occasionally move. Ask the head of year for the Year 11 calendar at the start of the year rather than discovering it a fortnight at a time.

sections.heading: Mock season, resits and the November option
paragraphs: Year 11 mocks reorganise the spring term and a plan that ignores them wastes money twice: during, when sessions compete with revision for tomorrow's paper, and after, by missing the week that is worth more than any other. Both are avoidable by deciding in advance rather than reacting.

During mocks, pause. The exception is a session aimed precisely at the paper being sat tomorrow, which can work if the tutor will abandon their plan to do it. The week after results is the one to protect and to book early, because for the first time there is a marked script. One hour going through it question by question with the student establishes whether the losses are method marks not written, non-calculator slowness, a topic genuinely unlearned, or time running out, and those are four different problems with four different remedies.

Then there is the resit question, which is worth understanding before results rather than after. UAE candidates sit the June series and the November series, and November functions as a resit route inside the same academic year for both main awarding bodies. The February and March series that circulates in online revision material is offered to India only and should not appear in a Dubai plan at all.

The published record shows the rhythm: Pearson's November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, with November 2025 results reaching students on 22 January 2026, while June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. Those are past dates, cited so the pattern is visible. For anything ahead use the awarding body's live timetable, and use only the timetable your school issues, because Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and warns that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone's version.

sections.heading: KHDA, the mandatory subjects and the evening that is fuller than it looks
paragraphs: Dubai's private schools are overseen by KHDA, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, described on u.ae as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, with annual inspection on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak. For a household here, the secondary mathematics commentary inside a report is more useful than the headline band, and it is a free second opinion on whether a weak grade reflects the student or the department.

The scheduling fact is the mandatory UAE subjects, which run alongside IGCSE rather than instead of it. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year. It also requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, stating that combined classes are strictly prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ.

Instructional time for those subjects is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least twenty-five minutes. For a Year 11 carrying nine examined subjects as well, the effect is fewer free periods in the school day, which means more work comes home and the two or three free evenings this page keeps referring to are carrying more than a parent assumes.

That is the argument for dovetailing rather than adding, and for ten minutes of extra practice rather than thirty. On credentials, plainly: IB Gram is not KHDA approved, ADEK approved or accredited by Cambridge, Pearson or Oxford AQA, and does not claim to be. A KHDA Educational Services Permit is a specific licence issued to training institutes with premises in Dubai, which is a different thing entirely from an individual tutor.

sections.heading: What we will not supply, whatever the week looks like
paragraphs: Two things are unavailable from us regardless of how tight a deadline has become. The first is assessed work. IGCSE maths has no coursework component in the main specifications, which removes most of the temptation here, but at least one operator ranking for UAE curriculum queries sells completed assessed work in other subjects at a published price, and the students buying it are the same students. Submitting work that is not your own is malpractice and the consequence falls on the student rather than the seller.

The second is examination material. We do not reproduce or distribute Cambridge, Pearson or Oxford AQA syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables, and we do not host them for download. We reference them and link to the awarding body's own page. That is the lawful position and it is also more useful, because the official version is the current version while a stale file circulating in a parents' group is a reliable route to revising content that has been withdrawn.

There is a scheduling version of the same principle. We will not fill a week that is already full in order to look responsive. If a household asks for three maths sessions a week in February of Year 11, the honest answer is that the week cannot absorb them, that the school's own revision provision is probably covering the content, and that four surgical sessions aimed at the marked script will do more. We would rather give that answer and lose two thirds of the booking.

And we will say when the problem is not teaching at all. A student capped by a Core or Foundation entry who is answering everything correctly needs a conversation with the maths department rather than a tutor, and a student who cannot access half of a Higher tier paper may be in the wrong tier rather than behind in it. Both are visible in a single marked script, and both are worth more to a family than a term of sessions.

sections.heading: Getting started, and the three questions we ask first
paragraphs: Three questions decide the shape of the arrangement and we ask them before proposing anyone. What does the school set for maths homework, and on which nights. What fixed commitments sit in the week, including clubs, fixtures and music. And what free revision provision does the school run, which in Year 11 changes how many paid hours are worth buying at all.

Then the specifics: the awarding body and specification code from the examinations officer, the tier, the latest grade labelled as mock or classwork, the teacher's last comment quoted rather than summarised, and a photograph of one marked script. The script is the most useful item by a distance, because it distinguishes method-mark losses from non-calculator slowness from content that was never learned, and those need different work.

We run the free trial lesson in the hour you would actually use rather than a convenient showcase slot, and we run it on the school's own homework where possible, because that is what a dovetailed arrangement looks like in practice. Afterwards, ask the tutor what the school set last week and what the error pattern was. A tutor who cannot answer the first question is proposing a parallel track.

And the honest part. The early-evening Gulf Standard Time hours this district wants fill first, and the week after mock results is the most contested booking of the year. When the hour you need is unavailable we say so and offer another evening, a weekend morning, or a tutor based outside the UAE working to Gulf Standard Time, disclosed as such. We will also say when the school's own provision is enough, which costs us the booking and is sometimes the right advice.

process.title: Tell us what the school sets, and when
process.description: Maths homework on three to five nights is the single biggest constraint on a tutoring plan. Knowing which nights it falls on lets us place the session where it improves that work rather than competing with it for the same twenty minutes.

process.title: Send the specification code and tier
process.description: One email to the examinations officer. The code determines whether nightly non-calculator practice is examinable preparation or wasted effort, and the tier determines the grade range, which is worth reviewing in Year 10 rather than Year 11.

process.title: Send one marked script
process.description: It distinguishes method-mark losses, which move in weeks, from non-calculator slowness, which takes a term, from content never learned, which takes longer still. Those are different plans and a grade alone cannot tell them apart.

process.title: Place the session before the homework
process.description: A session ending at half past five lets a student apply a correction to that night's work immediately, which is when it sticks. A session at seven leaves the homework already done wrongly and the correction untested for a week.

process.title: Free trial on the school's own work
process.description: We run the trial in the hour you intend to book and, where possible, on the homework the school has already set. Afterwards, ask the tutor what the error pattern was. A specific answer is the point of paying for a trained marker.

process.title: Act a year earlier than feels necessary
process.description: A Year 10 block of eight sessions achieves more than a Year 11 block of eight, because fluency needs a term to compound. If your child is in Year 10 and coping, that is the cheapest moment in the whole course to fix something.

whyPoints.title: Dovetailed, not duplicated
whyPoints.description: School maths sets work most nights, so our session marks that work and teaches from the errors rather than adding a parallel exercise sheet. It costs the same, the student does the work, and the improvement shows up where the department can see it.

whyPoints.title: Year 10 and Year 11 treated differently
whyPoints.description: Year 10 supports an algebra block that has time to compound; Year 11 supports four to six surgical sessions after mock results and little else. Selling the same product in both years is why so many Year 11 arrangements disappoint.

whyPoints.title: The twenty-minute rule
whyPoints.description: A student who has been in school since half past seven cannot start work the moment they walk in. Building in twenty minutes costs nothing and makes the same hour worth considerably more, which is the cheapest improvement on this page.

whyPoints.title: We tell you to use the school first
whyPoints.description: In Year 11, schools here run revision provision delivered by the teachers who entered your child. Duplicating it is the commonest avoidable waste, and we would rather lose the booking than charge for work being done free on a Wednesday.

whyPoints.title: No journey at either end
whyPoints.description: An online session begins when the student is settled rather than when a tutor has cleared afternoon traffic and gated access, which in this district is about forty-five minutes of the hour the evening can least afford.

whyPoints.title: Tier questions raised, not billed around
whyPoints.description: A student capped by their entry or unable to access half a paper has a placement problem rather than a teaching one, and both are visible in one marked script. We say so even though saying so ends the arrangement.

faqs.question: My child already gets maths homework most nights. Does a tutor just add more?
faqs.answer: A poor arrangement does, and the student then does whichever work gets collected, which is the school's. A good arrangement dovetails instead: the tutor marks the homework the school has already set, arrives knowing the error pattern, teaches that pattern, and sends the student back to the school's own work with a correction to apply. Nothing is added to the evening, the improvement appears in classwork the department actually sees, and at most ten minutes of extra practice is set on any night.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether a tutor is dovetailing or running a parallel track?
faqs.answer: Ask what the school set for maths last week. A tutor who cannot answer has not looked, which means they are teaching their own sequence alongside the school's and competing for the same twenty minutes of a crowded evening. Ask also what the error pattern in that work was. The point of paying a trained marker is that they say the student is slow at rearranging rather than that the student struggled with question seven, and that distinction is audible immediately.

faqs.question: Is Year 10 or Year 11 the right time to start maths tutoring?
faqs.answer: Year 10, by a wide margin, and most households ask in Year 11. A Year 10 week has three or four free evenings, no mock season and no school revision programme occupying the evenings, so algebraic fluency has a term or two to build. The same work compressed into February of Year 11 is triage rather than fluency-building. If your child is in Year 10 and merely coping, that is the cheapest moment in the entire two-year course to fix something.

faqs.question: What time should a maths session start from this district?
faqs.answer: Twenty minutes after your child gets home, which is between roughly 3:30pm and 4:50pm depending on the school. A student inside the district or in Nad Al Sheba is ready by about four; one travelling from Al Safa or Al Barsha not until nearly half past four. With an in-home tutor add about forty-five minutes throughout, because the tutor meets the same traffic and then the gated access here, which pushes school maths homework towards nine o'clock.

faqs.question: Why does twenty minutes before the session matter so much?
faqs.answer: Because a student who has been in school since half past seven cannot start working the moment they walk through the door. They need to put a bag down, eat and stop being in transit. A session booked for the minute of arrival buys an hour of someone physically present and mentally elsewhere, which is the most expensive hour in this market. Twenty minutes later the same hour is worth considerably more, and arranging it costs nothing at all.

faqs.question: Should the session be before or after homework?
faqs.answer: Before, where the week allows. A session ending at half past five lets a student apply the correction to that night's maths homework immediately, which is when a correction actually embeds. A session at seven leaves the homework already done, probably with the same error that was just discussed, and the correction waits a week to be tested on anything. It is a small sequencing point and it changes how fast a pattern gets fixed.

faqs.question: Should I use the school's revision classes before hiring anyone in Year 11?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the step most households skip. Schools serving this district typically run lunchtime clinics, spring-term after-school sessions and department past-paper workshops, delivered by the teachers who entered your child for the specification and wrote the mock. That provision is inside fees you already pay. Paid tutoring should start where it stops, by adding individual diagnosis and marked practice, rather than re-covering topics on a Thursday that the department covers free on a Wednesday.

faqs.question: How many maths sessions can a Year 11 week absorb?
faqs.answer: One weekly session, or a short bounded block, and rarely more. A Year 11 carries nine subjects setting work, mock examinations, school revision provision occupying some evenings and coursework deadlines in other subjects. Two or three paid maths sessions a week in February do not add teaching; they displace the revision and homework that the school is marking. The surgical block of four to six sessions after mock results is the format that genuinely fits.

faqs.question: Does my child's awarding body change what the nightly practice should be?
faqs.answer: Substantially. Under the Cambridge syllabus in use from 2025 each tier pairs a non-calculator paper with a calculator paper, so nightly arithmetic and algebra drill is examinable preparation. Pearson Edexcel Specification A permits a calculator in both papers, so the useful nightly work is short multi-step problems with the method written out instead. Ask the examinations officer for the code; a tutor drilling mental arithmetic for a Pearson candidate is spending your child's evenings on a skill the paper never tests.

faqs.question: What do we do during the mock fortnight?
faqs.answer: Pause, unless the session can be aimed at the paper being sat tomorrow and the tutor will abandon their plan to do it. During mocks the evenings belong to the next morning's examination and a general maths hour will be cancelled late or resented. What should be booked, months in advance, is the week after results, because for the first time there is a marked script and a diagnosis can be made from evidence rather than impression. That week is the most contested of the year here.

faqs.question: Can my child resit maths in November, and when do we decide?
faqs.answer: Yes. UAE candidates sit the June and November series, and November functions as a resit route inside the same academic year for both main awarding bodies. Entry goes through the school's examinations officer shortly after summer results, so the decision window is short. The published pattern is instructive: Pearson's November 2026 timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026 and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. The preparation window is roughly eight to ten weeks.

faqs.question: Which exam timetable should we work from?
faqs.answer: Only the one the school issues. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, warning that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone timetable. A timetable found online may belong to another zone entirely. Ask the examinations officer which zone your centre is in, and for future series open the awarding body's live timetable rather than a restatement of it.

faqs.question: Are holiday sessions worth it, or should they rest?
faqs.answer: Holidays are the most underused usable time in the whole course, and three to five sessions across a holiday week do more than the same number squeezed into term. Nothing competes, the student is rested, and a foundation gap can be addressed properly rather than between homework. That is different from a holiday programme filling every day, which produces diminishing returns. If the family travels, sessions follow the student, with the time zone agreed in advance so nobody works at six in the morning.

faqs.question: Is the school timetable really as full as you say?
faqs.answer: Fuller than most parents assume, because the mandatory UAE subjects run alongside IGCSE. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with requirements implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year and separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in several of them, calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit. The effect is fewer free periods, so more work comes home, which is why we dovetail rather than add.

faqs.question: What if the problem turns out to be the tier rather than the teaching?
faqs.answer: We say so, even though it ends the arrangement. A student capped by a Core or Foundation entry who answers everything correctly needs a conversation with the maths department, not a tutor. A student who cannot access half of a Higher tier paper may be in the wrong tier rather than behind in it. Both are visible in one marked script, and raising either in Year 10 with evidence is worth more to a household than a term of weekly sessions would be.

faqs.question: What should I send so the arrangement fits the week?
faqs.answer: Three things about the week and three about the subject. Which nights the school sets maths homework; the fixed commitments including clubs and fixtures; and what revision provision the school runs, if your child is in Year 11. Then the awarding body and specification code, the tier, and a photograph of one marked script. The script is worth more than the grade, because it tells us whether we are fixing a habit, a speed problem or a genuine content gap.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-mohammed-bin-.closingHeading: Make the homework they already have count
dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-mohammed-bin-.closingBody: Your child's evening already contains maths. The cheapest improvement available is not another hour of exercises but an hour that marks the work the school has set, names the error pattern and sends the student back to the same homework with a correction to apply. Tell us which nights the school sets maths, what the week already contains, the specification code and the tier, and send one marked script. We will propose a tutor and run the trial in the hour you would really use, on your child's own work.

intro.heading: Most lost marks are cheap marks given away
paragraphs: Open any marked IGCSE mathematics mock and count the lost marks by question size. For a student in the fours and fives, the pattern is almost always the same: a substantial share of the loss sits in the one and two-mark questions at the start of the paper, not in the long multi-part problems at the end. Those early questions are the cheapest marks on the paper. They are also the ones a student skims, miscopies, rounds wrongly or leaves half-finished because they are keen to reach the parts that feel like real mathematics.

That is a strategy problem rather than a knowledge problem, and strategy is faster to change than content. A student who banks every available cheap mark, follows a time budget, and answers the paper in an order that suits them can gain a grade without learning a single new topic. For a family in Motor City deciding how to spend a term, that is usually the first thing to buy and almost never the thing that gets bought, because it does not feel like tutoring: there is no new topic at the end of it, only a paper worked more carefully than it was before.

The second category is time. Most IGCSE mathematics papers print the total marks and the total minutes, which means a marks-per-minute rate can be calculated in ten seconds and used as a checkpoint. A student who knows they should be roughly halfway through the marks at the halfway point can self-correct during the paper. A student who has never done that arithmetic discovers at the end that the last two multi-part questions are blank, and loses more marks there than anywhere else on the paper.

The third is order. Nothing requires a paper to be answered front to back. A student who is strong on statistics and weak on trigonometry should take the statistics questions early while they are fresh and the clock is generous, and meet the trigonometry with whatever time and composure remain rather than the reverse. Teaching that is a single session and it changes a student's whole relationship with a timed paper, and it transfers to every other subject sat that summer rather than staying inside mathematics.

Motor City is a good place to work on all three, because GEMS Metropole School is inside the community and the school run is short. Students are often home by about half past three, which makes a 16:30 session realistic — and early sessions are better for this kind of drill than late ones. Teaching is delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time with a shared whiteboard, sessions run 45 or 60 minutes to 21:00, and there are no home visits anywhere in the UAE.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-motor-city.subjectsIntro: IGCSE mathematics topic areas as they appear on a paper, with the mark sizes each tends to attract. Reading a marked script against this list shows where the cheap marks are being lost.

subjects.name: Number and arithmetic
subjects.description: Standard form, ratio, proportion, bounds and estimation, usually set as one and two-mark questions early in a paper. These are the cheapest marks available and among the most frequently given away through miscopying or rounding partway through a calculation.

subjects.name: Percentages and reverse percentages
subjects.description: Increase, decrease, compound growth, depreciation and reverse percentages, appearing at both short and medium mark sizes. Reverse percentage questions are the reliable trap because students divide by the wrong base figure, and a multiplier method avoids both that and rounding error.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation
subjects.description: Expanding, factorising, simplifying algebraic fractions and rearranging formulae, set across every mark size. The single largest source of lost marks on an Extended paper and almost always a fluency problem carried up from Key Stage 3 rather than a gap in teaching.

subjects.name: Equations and inequalities
subjects.description: Linear, simultaneous and quadratic equations plus inequalities and regions. Quadratics attract medium mark allocations and students lose marks by giving a decimal where an exact form was asked for, or by discarding a valid negative root without reason.

subjects.name: Graphs and functions
subjects.description: Sketching, reading values, gradients of tangents and describing transformations. Transformation descriptions need a vector for a translation and a factor with a direction for a stretch, and vague wording loses the mark even when the drawn curve is correct.

subjects.name: Trigonometry and bearings
subjects.description: Right-angled trigonometry, then the sine and cosine rules and triangle area on Extended. Bearings questions produce disproportionate loss because the diagram is drawn carelessly, and choosing between the rules is itself the marked skill on non-right-angled problems.

subjects.name: Mensuration and compound shapes
subjects.description: Areas, volumes, surface areas, arcs and sectors, and problems combining several solids. Attracts the larger mark allocations. Units, premature rounding and forgetting that a composite volume may require a subtraction are the standing errors.

subjects.name: Probability and set notation
subjects.description: Tree diagrams, conditional probability on Extended, Venn diagrams and set notation. Set notation questions are short and almost pure recall of the symbols, which makes them cheap marks that students concede by not learning the notation.

subjects.name: Statistics and data
subjects.description: Averages from frequency tables, cumulative frequency, histograms with unequal class widths and box plots. Histogram frequency density is the recurring weak point, and interpretation questions want a comparison in context rather than a bare figure.

subjects.name: Vectors and matrices
subjects.description: Column vectors, magnitude, vector geometry on a diagram and matrix operations. Taught late in many schemes of work and consequently under-practised before mocks, which makes it a topic where cheap column-vector marks are lost alongside the harder geometry ones.

sections.heading: Cheap marks and expensive marks
paragraphs: Every IGCSE mathematics paper prints the mark allocation beside each question, and that number is the most useful piece of information on the page. A one-mark question wants one thing: a value, a term, a symbol. A two-mark question usually wants a method and an answer. A four or five-mark question wants a sequence, and a six-mark question in a multi-part structure usually depends on something established earlier. Treating all of them with the same care is the default and it is the wrong strategy.

Cheap marks are cheap because they require little and are quick to secure. Standard form conversions, a single percentage change, reading a value off a cumulative frequency curve, writing a set-notation symbol, stating a bound. A competent student can bank each of these in under a minute. A student in a hurry can also lose each of them in under a minute, by miscopying a figure, rounding at the wrong point, or answering a slightly different question from the one asked.

Expensive marks are the multi-part problems, usually later in the paper, where part (a) feeds part (b) and the whole structure can collapse from one early slip. These are worth more in total and they are where a student should be spending time — but only after the cheap marks are banked, because the arithmetic of the paper rewards certainty before ambition. A student who spends twenty minutes on a six-mark question and then rushes eight one-mark questions has made a poor trade.

The diagnostic that makes this visible is simple and worth doing once. Take a marked mock and total the lost marks in two columns: questions worth one or two marks, and questions worth three or more. For most students in the fours and fives, the first column is larger than they expect and sometimes larger than the second. That single number is usually enough to change how a student approaches the next paper.

sections.heading: Building a time budget from the paper's own front page
paragraphs: The front page of a mathematics paper gives the total marks and the time allowed. Dividing one by the other gives a marks-per-minute rate, and that rate is the only pacing tool a student needs. It takes ten seconds at the start of the paper and it converts a vague anxiety about time into a checkable number: at the halfway point, roughly half the marks should be behind you.

The reason this works is that it is self-correcting during the paper rather than afterwards. A student who reaches the halfway point with a third of the marks done knows, at that moment, to change behaviour — to stop polishing, to move past a question that is not yielding, to bank the cheap marks further on and return if time allows. A student without the rate discovers the problem when they turn the final page with eleven minutes left and two multi-part questions untouched.

The budget also needs a rule for abandoning a question, which most students do not have. A sensible one is that if a question has consumed roughly double its mark value in minutes and is not resolving, it gets a mark in the margin and a return visit later. Students resist this because leaving something unfinished feels like failure, which is exactly why it has to be practised under timed conditions rather than merely explained.

The last element is the final sweep. Reserving the last few minutes to revisit flagged questions and to check that every question has at least something written against it is worth more than attempting one more hard part. An empty answer earns nothing; a partially correct method often earns something. That habit alone accounts for a meaningful number of marks across a paper and costs no mathematics at all.

sections.heading: Answering in an order that suits the student
paragraphs: Papers are printed in an order that suits the examiner's structure, not the individual student's strengths. Nothing in the rubric requires front-to-back answering, and for a student with an uneven topic profile the order is a lever worth using. Someone strong on statistics and weak on trigonometry should meet the statistics questions early, while the clock is generous and concentration is high, rather than arriving at them with eight minutes left.

The practical method is a thirty-second scan at the start. Turn through the paper, mark the questions that look immediately doable, and start there. The marks banked in the first fifteen minutes are the most reliable marks on the paper, and the confidence they produce measurably improves performance on the harder questions afterwards — a student who has already secured twenty marks approaches a difficult problem differently from one who has not yet secured any.

There are two cautions. The first is administrative: answers must be written in the correct place for the question, and a student jumping around the paper has to be disciplined about that. The second is that jumping should be a plan rather than a panic. A student who moves on every time a question looks hard ends up with a paper of fragments. The scan happens once, the order is set, and the abandon rule handles everything after that.

This is one session to teach and two or three timed papers to embed, which makes it one of the highest-return interventions available in the final term. It also transfers to every other examination the student sits that summer, which is a reasonable argument for buying it early in the revision period rather than late.

sections.heading: What each grade actually signals, and what the tier allows
paragraphs: Cambridge IGCSE results come on a 9-1 numeric scale with 9 highest, alongside legacy A*-G reporting on some syllabuses and in some regions. Parents who sat GCSEs themselves tend to map the numbers onto the old letters incorrectly, usually assuming 9 corresponds exactly to A* and 7 to B. The scales were set so that the numeric grades spread the top end more finely, so the mapping is not one to one, and what matters in practice is the threshold the receiving school states and the scale it states it in.

What a grade signals is mostly about which doors it opens. A sixth form offering A Level Mathematics commonly asks for grade 6 or 7 in the subject. An IB school offering Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches expects comparable algebraic fluency, whether or not it names a number. A grade 4 or 5 is a pass that will satisfy a Ministry of Education equivalency requirement — five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count — without opening a mathematics route at sixteen.

The tier of entry sits underneath all of this and is the constraint families most often discover late. A Cambridge Core entry is commonly capped at grade 5 or C, and no performance lifts a result above the cap. A student aiming at an A Level that wants grade 6 therefore needs an Extended entry, and the school decides entries on internal evidence gathered across Year 10, months before the papers are sat.

Which makes the mark economy described on this page tier-dependent in one specific way. For a student on Extended aiming at grade 6 or 7, strategy work on cheap marks and pacing is often the difference. For a student on Core already near the cap, the same work secures the grade but cannot raise the ceiling, and the useful conversation is instead about whether the tier itself should change — which is a Year 10 conversation requiring marked Extended-standard evidence.

sections.heading: The habits underneath the strategy
paragraphs: Strategy only pays if the underlying habits are in place, because a student who has to think hard about rearranging a formula has no spare attention for pacing. There are four habits that matter and all four are procedural rather than conceptual, which means they can be installed on a known timescale and verified afterwards.

The first is writing method as it is produced. Method marks exist on every mathematics paper and are awarded for visible steps, so a student who computes a chain of operations on a calculator and writes only the final figure forfeits them when the answer is right and loses everything when it is wrong. One intermediate value per line. Two sessions to install, and it holds.

The second is rounding once, at the end. Carry full precision through every intermediate step and round only the final answer to the accuracy the question specifies. Rounding partway puts the final value outside the accepted tolerance, so the mark goes even though the method was sound — which is the loss students find most unfair and which is entirely avoidable.

The third is checking part (a) before continuing. On a multi-part question an early error propagates through every later part, so thirty seconds spent sanity-checking part (a) protects the four or five marks that depend on it. The fourth is reading the question twice, which sounds trivial and is the single commonest cause of lost cheap marks: answering a near-miss version of what was asked. Each of these is two sessions, and together they typically account for more recoverable marks than any individual topic.

sections.heading: What the strategy work costs, and when to buy it
paragraphs: Strategy work is cheap relative to content teaching and it has a fixed length, which makes it unusually easy to cost. A mark-economy block is four to six sessions. The four procedural habits are four to six between them, with overlap. A timed-paper run is one full paper a fortnight with a session to mark each, so six sessions covers a term. None of those expands to fill whatever is bought, which content teaching reliably does.

Because the work has a fixed length, the published Dubai bands are more usefully read as block totals than as hourly rates. Take a five-session mark-economy block. Bestimate's 2026 rate table puts qualified online subject tutors at AED 150-300 an hour, so that block is AED 750 to 1,500, paid once rather than monthly. The same table gives AED 180-350 for in-home one-to-one and AED 200-450 or above for IGCSE and IB specialists, with independent home tutors reaching AED 500 once travel is included. TutorChase at AED 270 makes the block AED 1,350; BartyED at AED 650 at the premium end makes it AED 3,250. Read as totals on a finite job, the distance between the bands is a one-off difference of a few thousand dirhams rather than a standing commitment, which is the whole argument for buying strategy work instead of open-ended content teaching. There is a reason to spend at the qualified band rather than the entry band for this particular work. Marking a paper against a published scheme and separating cheap-mark loss from content loss requires somebody who has read those schemes and knows what a method mark looks like. A tutor at the entry band may teach the topic competently and be unable to tell a student why a correct answer scored one out of three, which is exactly the information the block is buying.

On timing, buy it before the final six weeks. Strategy needs two or three timed papers to embed, and a student meeting the abandon rule for the first time a fortnight before the series will not trust it under pressure. sections.heading: The dates and the series a Motor City candidate should know
paragraphs: Strategy work has to be placed against real dates, and several of the relevant ones are not the examination itself. The centre's entry deadline falls months before the first paper and fixes the board, the syllabus code and the tier. The mock window is the school's and produces the marked script this whole page depends on. The zone timetable arrives ahead of the series. And results day sits well after the final paper.

The published positions. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The February/March series is offered to India only, so no UAE candidate sits it and a plan built around a March window is built on a date that does not apply. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November; the November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so open the live official timetable rather than trusting any restatement.

The administrative rule worth checking before printing anything: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable version, states that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone, and notes that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Ask the examinations officer which zone your centre is in.

And the Dubai-specific variable. Where Ramadan falls in the weeks before a June series, school hours shorten and the productive study window moves to after Iftar. Full timed papers should therefore be front-loaded into the earlier part of the spring, and the Ramadan weeks used for short review, recall and marking papers already sat. Sessions move to post-Iftar timing between 20:30 and 22:00 on request at no additional cost, and every session is recorded, so a student working late can revisit it the following day.
